text:
Can you tell when someone nearby is wearing Meta AI glasses?

As millions of people buy into the smart glasses fad each year, the odds are increasing that you could be secretly recorded while simply going about your day.

Meta is not the only smart glasses maker, but its AI glasses are by far the most popular. And as the devices become more common, some public places, including schools, courts, restaurants, and entertainment venues, have begun to ban them. Even tech lovers have rejected Meta glasses in certain settings. The hackers behind DEF CON 2026 reportedly banned smart glasses with no exceptions, reminding attendees with prescription pairs to "be sure to pack non-violating eyewear if you need them."

But a ban is only as effective as the people enforcing it. Spotting a pair of smart glasses can require tech-savvy security staff, and enforcement may depend on users voluntarily disclosing their devices-or on watchful observers speaking up.

Those bans are an important way to push back against the potential for abuse. But privacy advocates know that increasing the social friction around nonconsensual recording can't stop the practice by itself.

Until comprehensive consumer privacy laws are passed, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has warned that Meta seems prepared to make the tech even more invasive in its bid to sell more glasses and stay ahead of rivals in the burgeoning industry.

And as AI advances, EFF staff technologist Cooper Quintin told Ars, potential new features such as facial recognition could raise the stakes further, potentially allowing the devices to be used to create convincing deepfakes or nonconsensual intimate imagery of people who may not be aware that cameras are rolling.

"I think that there are a lot of other concerns there beyond just being recorded without your knowledge," Quintin told Ars.

EFF has warned that smart glasses makers will likely be tempted to add facial-recognition features unless lawmakers intervene and give people a private right to sue companies whose products violate their biometric privacy rights. In the meantime, the group has released a guide for smart-glasses users that lays out ways to resist facial recognition, develop responsible recording habits, and better understand the privacy risks of continuous recording. It also urges users to consider blurring strangers' faces before posting videos online.

For people unknowingly targeted in secret recordings, the only safety feature Meta provides is nearly "useless," Quintin told Ars.

A tiny recording light that can be easily covered with a sticker is unlikely to deter bad actors intent on abusing the glasses, whether stalkers or creepy partners secretly recording women in public bathrooms or private bedrooms. The tech has also controversially been used in immigration raids, 404 Media reported, and to harass sex workers and retail workers . And on social media, videos show a range of other unwanted recordings, from relatively inoffensive pranks to more harmful videos featuring bullying or harassment.

The volume of these videos online suggests the LED feature "is better than nothing, but not by much," Quintin said.

Hobbyists build apps to detect glasses

Experts have noted that Meta may already have plans to diminish that limited safety feature. The company is supposedly "testing a prototype of 'super sensing' AI glasses that would use cameras and audio recordings to capture a wearer's every moment," the Financial Times reported last month. According to sources familiar with Meta's thinking, executives "are planning not to activate the LED when the super-sensing features are being used," even though "that would make it harder for bystanders to know when they were being recorded."

Meta execs' plans may change if the public's privacy concerns remain a sticking point, though, sources have suggested. And backlash will likely be sustained as more people wear the glasses, since digital rights experts have accused Meta of failing to consider civil rights or privacy ramifications when designing new features. Perhaps most troublingly, Meta recently backpedaled and deleted an unreleased facial recognition system from its smart-glasses app that Wired and EFF revealed had been quietly installed on 50 million phones in June.

It's unclear if or when Meta might try to bring the facial recognition system back. Meta did not respond to Ars' request to comment on this story.

As Meta glasses have become more commonplace, hobbyist programmers have been building apps to detect when smart glasses are nearby so people can steer clear of them.

These civil defense apps, Quintin said, aren't a perfect solution to the social problem of smart-glasses recording without consent. But when used in combination with bans, the apps can offer wary members of the public a way to check if a ban is being enforced or whether a nearby device may begin recording at a sensitive time. Society needs both solutions, Quintin said, especially because the most popular and recognizable smart glasses available today will likely one day come in a wider assortment of trendy models, making them harder to spot in the wild.

"You need to have the social construct around these being unwelcome, and you also need to be able to find when people are using these," Quintin said. "Right now, they're pretty easy to just detect with your eyes. They're pretty obvious, but that might not always be the case. So technologies like this are also important to supplement that."

"I can do something about it"

Since February, engineers have been releasing and updating apps that help people detect glasses like Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, or Snap Spectacles.

"It is completely unsurprising that people are building apps to fight back against Meta glasses and other surreptitious public recording," Quintin told Ars. Many people "have a deep revulsion to being recorded without their consent, which is understandable," and that remains "the biggest problem with these glasses," Quintin said.

Smart-glasses detector apps aren't perfect. At best, they can alert users when nearby glasses are turned on by detecting the Bluetooth signal used to pair the glasses with a phone. Most importantly, the apps cannot determine whether the glasses are actively recording, and users are cautioned to never assume that someone wearing smart glasses is recording them. App makers also advise against confrontation and accept no liability for false positives or misunderstandings. Additionally, detection may be unreliable if a wall or other obstacle, like a human body, interferes with a signal.

Users don't seem to consider these flaws deal-breakers. They simply want some way to scan a room, and some are eager to provide feedback to improve the apps, even expressing an emotional investment in seeing the technology develop.

One of the first apps, Nearby Glasses, is available for $2.99 on both iOS and Android. It has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store and remains the most popular such app, despite the developer, Yves Jeanrenaud, warning on GitHub that he's "no pro developer" and that "detecting Bluetooth LE devices might sometimes just not work as expected," and "false positives are likely."

Released in response to online content showing that smart glasses are "an intolerable intrusion, consent neglecting, horrible piece of tech," Jeanrenaud said, he kept his goals humble. On GitHub, he wrote that "I hope this app is useful for someone," but "I do not want to promote techsolutionism, nor do I want people to feel falsely secure. It's still an imperfect approach," and it probably "always will be."

By July, another detector, Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner, was nearing the top of iPhone charts, also charging $3 for the service. One high school teacher reviewing the app called it the "best $3 I've spent," writing that she was concerned that her students could use AI glasses to take unwanted recordings in class.

Ars tested the most recently released app, Zuckoff, which launched for free on iPhone in early August and is currently seeking 12 testers to launch on Android devices later this year.

Already, thousands of users have downloaded the iPhone app, with some eagerly submitting feedback that has helped improve key functionality, including the ability to detect AI glasses and receive alerts when the app is closed. Perpetual scanning is an optional feature that costs about $10 a year. The subscription helps cover the costs of "continuous support" for the app, Zuckoff's creator, Pawel Szydlowski, told Ars.

Like Jeanrenaud's app, Zuckoff collects no data and was created partly in response to toxic Meta glasses content flooding social media. Szydlowski told Ars that he built the app in one week after finishing another project that scans for nearby Bluetooth devices and deciding, "Let's see how far we can go with detecting those glasses."

Without researching whether other apps had already sought to solve the problem, Szydlowski decided to put his 10 years of iPhone developer experience to work. "I was like, 'I can do something about it, so let's go,'" Szydlowski told Ars.

Building a Meta glasses detector

Szydlowski's biggest challenge was collecting the unique identifiers that manufacturers use to label different products for regulatory purposes. Zuckoff uses these identifiers to help users detect specific smart-glasses models while ignoring Bluetooth signals from less creepy devices. To compile as comprehensive a list as possible, Szydlowski crawled Instagram and Reddit for photos of people wearing different types of smart glasses.

"I see you have those glasses," Szydlowski would say in messages to early Meta glasses adopters, who agreed to help despite presumably approving of the technology. "Can you help me with this little name? I want to know the unique identifier that's broadcasting."

To catch glasses with identifiers that Zuckoff hasn't yet logged, Szydlowski created a workaround that first flags devices by their advertised names. It's less precise, he said, but it gives users some indication that a pair of smart glasses may be nearby, even without a known identifier. He's currently working on another solution that should widen discovery even further, he told Ars.

Szydlowski's app first alerted him to nearby smart glasses when he ran into two colleagues wearing them at a recent Apple event in Poland. That helped him confirm the tech was working as he hoped.

When you load Zuckoff, the app "estimates distance from signal strength and puts a confidence level on every hit rather than a hard yes or no," Szydlowski explained. Esitmates tell users if glasses are very close (within arm's length), close (in the same room), near (nearby) and far.  This feature also makes it possible to see when you may be approaching an area with a larger concentration of smart glasses, like in a tourist trap such as the Las Vegas strip.

Ars replicated the test, thanks to this writer's brother-in-law, who agreed to use the app to detect his own Ray-Bans. He likes to use his smart glasses to record nature sightings when he goes boating or to take action shots of his bulldog playing fetch along the lake, and he had the glasses on him when I called to see if he could run the test.

After putting the glasses on, my brother-in-law loaded the app, which detected the glasses in minutes and warned that "one possible pair" was "within arm's length." (In this case, the message was very literal, since he was wearing the glasses while looking at the phone in his hand.)

The app then references the identifier to help the user detect exactly which model is nearby, and my brother-in-law confirmed that Zuckoff correctly labeled his smart glasses.

For Szydlowski, the toughest challenge was figuring out how Apple might allow the app to run in the background, since the company is "very strict when it comes to apps working in the background all the time." He worried some users wouldn't find the app as beneficial without that functionality. Eventually, he settled on a solution that scans continuously, but rather than flagging all known devices the moment they're turned on, Apple allows only a fixed list of known Bluetooth service identifiers to be detected in that mode. Extra-cautious users should therefore also open the app to see the full list of potential devices in the area.

"This background feature, it's so crucial," Szydlowski said.

Android may allow him to offer faster detection through background functionality, Szydlowski suggested, because unlike Apple devices, Android allows background activities to be "possible to exempt from battery optimization," Szydlowski said. That means Zuckoff "can continue using the battery in the background" without Android protocols that "wipe out the apps that are consuming your battery," he said.

Although people have mostly grown accustomed to the idea of being recorded without consent in public, smart glasses have the potential to expand mass surveillance in ways that deeply concern privacy advocates.

Meta could introduce technical solutions, like automatically blurring faces, as Google does in Street View images, but Szydlowski doubts Meta would voluntarily make such a privacy-conscious change without regulatory or public pressure. The creator of Zuckoff, a name that takes a cheeky dig at Meta's founder, also said that "I'm pretty sure they're not going to be happy with this app existing."

He likens malicious smart-glasses recording to the earliest harms of Apple's AirTags. When that technology was released in 2021, the easy-to-hide tracking devices were soon implicated in stalking cases. But there still is no federal law targeting AirTag abuses, and it took the first states to act on the emerging privacy threat roughly three to five years to pass legislation prohibiting the invasive tracking.

Szydlowski worries lawmakers will be similarly slow to react to threats from Meta glasses. He told Ars he thinks the best solution might be rules mandating companies like Meta to advertise a specific Bluetooth service identifier while recording. That would improve civil defense apps like his.

In the meantime, he hopes people will find the detector app that they like best and use it to spread awareness of the risk that smart glasses may be present in a room where they're unexpected or explicitly forbidden.

"The goal of this app was just making people aware because a lot of people won't be aware until it becomes a major problem, which was the case with AirTags, basically," Szydlowski said.

Meta expects demand to explode

Last December, analysts forecasted that 2026 would be a breakthrough year for smart glasses. And it's clear by now that Meta wants this to be the year that AI glasses are suddenly everywhere you look.

The tech giant invested heavily in promoting them, collaborating with celebrity influencer Kylie Jenner on a pair of Ray-Bans featuring an AI assistant that speaks in her voice. The campaign featured billboard ads and a video spot showing Kylie simply enjoying wearing the glasses, without necessarily highlighting their practical features. The partnership was rumored to have paid Jenner millions of dollars and was intended to position the technology as a fashionable, practical accessory-and perhaps buff out the public perception of them as "pervert glasses." But critics have argued that the ads seem narrowly designed to encourage more people to use their glasses for continuous recording.

Though the Jenner campaign was supposedly viewed as a success internally at Meta, it also prompted global backlash. On social media, the protest collective "Everyone Hates Elon" razed Jenner, The Huffington Post reported, saying that "recording everything we see and do constantly? It's giving fascism, not fashion," "hun." And pop singer Lorde stopped a festival performance to tell her fans, "Fuck the glasses. Don't get the glasses. Not sexy."

Salon's Andi Zeisler slammed the Kylie Edition glasses for trying to lull women into a false sense of security, even as Meta knows the technology has been used to record women without their knowledge, both in public and private. In London, activists took that criticism a step further, replacing bus stop ads of Jenner smiling in the glasses with a spoof in which her face transforms into a skeletal grin above the warning that at Meta, "We're always watching."

But despite protests, the glasses aren't going away any time soon, as Meta plans to move millions more into production. In 2025, the company sold more than 7 million AI glasses-up from 2 million sold in the prior two years combined-then quickly made plans to double its Ray-Ban outputs, Bloomberg reported. By the end of 2026, Meta expects to start producing at least 20 million glasses annually to meet demand, or perhaps as many as 30 million if the market continues trending strongly.

Beyond the backlash, regulating the glasses is a touchy subject, Quintin told Ars. No civil rights group would advocate banning recording in public, a practice that can be crucial for holding police and government officials accountable. What may prove just as useful as thoughtful privacy regulations, Quintin suggested, is a broader effort to ban the technology at the community level.

Szydlowski told Ars that he's personally not bothered by Meta's AI glasses, only by the gross content made with them. But other critics, like Quintin, think the tech is "disgusting" and "unacceptable," and he has little hope that technical solutions can solve the problem and abundant concern that the privacy risks will compound as enthusiasm for the technology grows.

Right now, there's less social friction around using glasses to record than there was when people first started using phones to record public interactions, Quintin suggested. As a father of young children, he recently saw another dad using glasses to film kids at a birthday party, a moment that illustrates how smart glasses have shifted the power dynamic.

Previously, "if you wanted to record somebody, you had to take out your phone, shove it in their face," Quintin said. "And they know they're being recorded. That is a useful social friction. And the glasses remove that and put the friction on the other end. The friction is now on me, calling you a pervert for wearing glasses and telling you to stop recording my kids."

Szydlowski somewhat agreed. He told Ars there's value in being able to record hands-free from eye level, but he created Zuckoff because he draws the line at posting harmful smart-glasses recordings online.

"People are using it in a bad way," Szydlowski said. "That was the first part that annoyed me. I was like, 'I don't like it. I just don't enjoy the content, and I don't think it's valid' because myself, I wouldn't have a way to react to being recorded because I'm used to people holding the phone and actually pointing at me. Then I can say, 'Hold on a second. This is not scrolling. Someone is actually recording.'"

text:
While traveling, Peggy Dahl developed a cough so bad it left her gasping for breath after each bout. Far from her doctor, and with a sneaking suspicion of bronchitis, she turned to ChatGPT.

This wasn't the first time she had used it as a medical sounding board.

During a visit to her daughter, the chatbot had correctly flagged symptoms of a urinary tract infection. On the last trip, ChatGPT ruled out bronchitis and urged her to find a professional. An X-ray at a nearby urgent care soon confirmed a case of pneumonia. Without ChatGPT, Dahl said, she probably would have delayed getting treatment.

"It was really good," Dahl said. "It just talks to you like your best friend."

Like Dahl, 29% of American adults say they use AI tools or chatbots for health information each month -- nearly double the number two years ago, according to June survey data from the health research firm KFF.

Medical experts see helpful and harmful outcomes from AI in consumer health. A health chatbot could provide clarity and more individualized guidance to patients. However, early research suggests an overreliance on AI could pose privacy risks or prevent people from seeking care when needed.

"There've been many technological innovations in health care in the last few decades, but this is by far the fastest adoption of anything I've seen," said Dr. Andrew Olson, a physician and professor at the University of Minnesota who has studied artificial intelligence in health care.

A decade ago, Olson said, patients were searching for symptoms on Google. Now, he sees AI tools loaded on their personal devices in the exam room. Some of the systems are designed to explain diagnoses, evaluate symptoms and inform patients, so they come to appointments with questions.

Tech companies are looking to cash in. Earlier this year, OpenAI and Amazon both launched health-focused chatbot features for uploading medical records, test results and fitness tracker data. In June, Microsoft announced a partnership with the Mayo Clinic to develop its own health-focused AI product.

Those AI models can be "empowering" when they distill dense medical data to provide accurate personalized information, triage new injuries and clarify obscure medical terms, said Martin Michalowski, an AI-focused researcher at the University of Minnesota's School of Nursing.

But he's wary of the limitations: models like ChatGPT work by predicting the most likely next words in a sentence based on the texts used to train them, not by holistically generating knowledge about a topic. And he advises patients to be cautious about providing data to a chatbot they might not be comfortable sharing publicly.

Besides privacy concerns, the medical results so far have been mixed. One study testing OpenAI's ChatGPT Health model found it underdiagnosed emergency cases about half the time. Last month, a Florida pastor sued OpenAI, claiming ChatGPT led him to delay care for a critical blood clot in his lungs.

Dr. Olson shares the concern that patients might blindly trust tools not designed for health care. He's wary of bias in chatbots that agree with whatever a user suggests, even if it's not medically accurate.

But he's also optimistic about new uses for AI in the clinic, especially when it can help patients better understand their own health or decide whether to make a long drive to a hospital.

"I think we should encourage people to advocate for their own health," Olson said. "You should look stuff up. And then you should talk about it with your health care provider."

When lawyer Marc Berris started feeling brain fog, he thought his clinical depression was getting worse. Swapping antidepressants didn't change his symptoms, and his primary care doctor was stumped.

But an AI tool flagged an important caveat. The 57-year-old from New Hope had recently seen other specialists who'd prescribed the drug topiramate for weight loss, and they hadn't warned him that brain fog was a possible side effect.

He brought this AI-powered theory to his primary care physician, who helped him swap topiramate for a GLP-1 medication. Soon after, Berris's brain fog lifted. Since then, he's used ChatGPT to build workout plans and find recipes to manage the nausea that can accompany the drugs.

"What I think [AI] is doing is creating more informed patients," Berris said. "Even if the information that I get through an AI tool is not spot-on, it's at least getting me to ask the right questions of my providers."

Berris doesn't think ChatGPT will replace his doctor anytime soon. He still trusts providers with a traditional medical school education over a machine learning model, he said.

But other patients are embracing AI to make health care decisions. St. Paul, Minnesota, resident Bryan Hayes, 62, has accumulated a lot of health care data over nearly a decade of dabbling in the DIY longevity movement known as biohacking.

Before, each test result was locked behind its own patient portal; now he has AI pore over his blood work, MRI results and lung scans together.

Hayes used Anthropic's Claude tool to build his own website, themed after the science fiction novel "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy," where he could upload and store his results. Hayes feeds in new data, and the website uses a Claude-powered agent named "Eddie" to analyze it and provide recommendations.

When he brought his AI-generated health report to a cardiologist to obtain a prescription for an uncommon cholesterol medication, he said the physician was intrigued.

"In 30 years, he had not ever seen anything quite like that," Hayes said.

After Henry Dorgan slipped on a spot of water in his bathroom and hyperextended his knee, he thought about making a doctor's appointment.

During his visit the month prior for a painful jaw disorder, the 31-year-old from Minneapolis felt frustrated to receive a prescription for a muscle relaxer, but no rehab options and a four-month wait to see a provider. For a knee injury, he guessed the costs of imaging and prescription drugs would add up fast.

So instead, he wrote a detailed message to Microsoft's Copilot AI chatbot, which he'd used at work. He offered his height, weight, injury description and pain levels, and Copilot shot back a possible diagnosis: a grade 1 patellar tendon strain.

As he updated the chat with symptoms, it adjusted his physical therapy plan. Dorgan was an avid runner, so Copilot suggested he might try a low-impact spin bike while he recovered. And if he experienced swelling, the chatbot said, he should see a doctor to check if the tendon was torn.

"It was extraordinarily descriptive," Dorgan said. "I probably saved hundreds of dollars in medical costs."

If he realized something was seriously wrong, Dorgan said he'd go straight to a doctor. But with rising health care costs and long wait times to see humans, he's among a new cadre of patients who plan on asking AI to triage symptoms and find savings.

Woodbury, Minnesota, resident Leigh Ann Ahmad, 51, turned to AI when she felt her optometrist dismissed symptoms of a growing blind spot in her eye. ChatGPT's triaging encouraged her to return with recommended follow-up questions. Her optometrist referred her to a specialist, who eventually diagnosed her with a long-hidden nerve disorder in her eye.

But then, she faced a new problem: a $5,000 bill for follow-up imaging her doctor recommended, but her insurance refused to cover.

ChatGPT helped her find the right words, she said. Based on its instructions, Ahmad asked the insurance agent about initiating an "appeal process." Something clicked: the insurance agent called her doctor's office to seek authorization, and the bill disappeared.

"When I used that (language) in the call with my insurance company, it was like night and day," Ahmad said. "I never had to fill out another form, or had to get another bill outstanding, or make another call."

text:
Turns out, the robots don't have all the answers.

The robots, like humans, can't see the future and tell us what is going to happen before it does. Even as the robot rebellion seemingly inches closer with each passing day thanks to the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), there are still some safe spaces left to hide.

One of them might just be in the world of NFL predictions.

Prior to the 2025 NFL season, we asked for some input from Google's Gemini about how the upcoming campaign would play out. We kept it fairly simple with record predictions that would paint a picture of the standings. We also kept that going with weekly picks from Microsoft's Copilot as an opportunity to see how well it tracked the ebbs and flows of a season.

2026 NFL RECORD PREDICTIONS: AI makes win-loss picks for all 32 teams

Copilot fared much better in that regard, posting a 177-94-1 record in the regular season and a 12-1 mark in the postseason.

With that in mind, maybe the takeaway is to ask for information in the moment. At least for the time being, the old-fashioned way of asking a human might be the best course of action for long-term NFL predictions, stock tips and other advice.

As the 2026 NFL season kickoff approaches, here's a look back at how AI did with it's 2025 season predictions.

AI predicts the 2025 NFL season, revisited

What AI got right

Gemini managed to correctly predict the record for just four of the league's 32 teams. If percentages are your thing, that is just 12.5% of the time – a hit rate that is far from inspiring.

The Buffalo Bills (12-5), Cleveland Browns (5-12), Philadelphia Eagles (11-6) and San Francisco 49ers (12-5) were the only teams to post the same record that the chatbot predicted before the season.

Did it get any division winners right?

One isn't just the loneliest number. It's also the number of division winners that Gemini got right from its preseason predictions in 2025.

The Eagles, at 11-6, were the NFC East champions in 2025 – even though the year was far from magical in Philadelphia. However, the competition, or lack thereof, in the division made the difference.

If moral victories are your thing, four of Gemini's predicted division champions finished as the second-place team so it's not all bad.

The Washington Commanders

Gemini was adamant about one thing prior to the 2025 season – the Commanders weren't going to have a good year. It was a break from the consensus about Dan Quinn's upstart bunch, led by the rookie of the year, Jayden Daniels. Injuries certainly didn't help Washington's outlook, but the chatbot was focused instead on the offseason moves.

The Commanders went all-in, but they went all-in on older veterans. Gemini said that the team could struggle to integrate those pieces, something that came to fruition almost instantly.

Washington finished with a 5-12 record, one less win than Gemini predicted during the offseason.

What AI got wrong

Well, everything else. Let's break it down.

What was AI's biggest miss?

Easy. The Seattle Seahawks.

Gemini predicted that the eventual Super Bowl champions would win just seven games and finish last in the NFC West. It's hard to fault the chatbot, however. The Seahawks weren't considered a contender heading into the season. They also weren't even considered a true contender until later in the season.

Seattle became an overnight juggernaut, despite "losing" some key pieces in trades ahead of the 2025 campaign. Turns out, the decision to trust Sam Darnold and Jaxon Smith-Njigba was a good one. Mike Macdonald's team went on to win 14 games and blazed through the playoffs without really breaking a sweat along the way.

What were some of the other misses?

Gemini was off by four or more games nine times. The chatbot underestimated the Patriots by five wins, Jaguars by four wins, Broncos by five wins and Seahawks by seven wins. It overestimated the Jets by four wins, Bengals by four wins, Chiefs by six wins, Giants by four wins and Cardinals by five wins.

It comes in 40mm and 44mm sizes. If you don't need a cellular plan, there's a Bluetooth-only Galaxy Watch 9 model. Like the original, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 comes in a single large 47mm size, with both Bluetooth and LTE baked in by default.  Left to right: Two Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 models, two sizes of the Galaxy Watch 9 (Credit: Eric Zeman)  The Galaxy Watch 9 starts at $379.99 for the Bluetooth-only 40mm model (a $30 price increase compared with the Galaxy Watch 8), while the 44mm model starts at $409.99. Add $50 to either size for the LTE-equipped variant.  The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 costs $699.99, a $50 increase over the original Ultra. That works out to a $320 premium over the base Galaxy Watch 9, or an extra $240 over the most expensive variant (the 44mm Watch 9 with LTE, which costs $459.99).  The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 comes in gray or silver. The 40mm Watch 9 is offered in graphite or cream, and the 44mm version is available in graphite or silver.  Winner: Galaxy Watch 9  Samsung Unveils Two New Galaxy Watches  Power: The Base Model Matches the Ultra  Both the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 have a new Qualcomm Snapdragon Wear Elite processor that offers better efficiency and increased CPU and GPU performance compared with the Exynos W1000 processor in the Galaxy Watch 8 and the original Ultra. The Ultra 2 has double the storage of the Watch 9, 64GB compared with 32GB, and both have 2GB of memory.  Both watches use Google's Wear OS 7 overlaid with Samsung's One UI 9, each one generation newer than what's currently available on older models, though the Galaxy Watch 8 and original Ultra could get the latest software via an update at some point.  While getting extra storage with the Ultra 2 is a nice bonus, this isn't the reason to spend the extra Benjamins. The Galaxy Watch 9 offers the same power for less.  Winner: Tie  Battery Life: The Main Reason to Pay More  The Ultra 2 has more battery capacity and lasts much longer than the Watch 9 between charges, and that's the main reason to spend more for the premium model if you're not into adventuring.  Specifically, the Ultra 2 has an 800mAh cell and an estimated battery life of 60 hours on a charge with the always-on display enabled. That's a sizable increase over the original Ultra, which has a 590mAh battery with an estimated 48 hours of power per charge. In testing, the Ultra 2 outlasted the company's estimate, running for an impressive 69.5 hours under normal use with the always-on display enabled, up from 46 hours for the original Ultra.  The Galaxy Watch 9 only lasts a day between charges (Credit: Joseph Maldonado)  Both Galaxy Watch 9 sizes have much smaller cells than the Ultra 2; the 40mm has 390mAh, while the 44mm has 445mAh. Both figures are larger than their respective Watch 8 counterparts (325mAh for the 40mm and 435mAh for the 44mm), but the Watch 9 has the same 30-hour battery estimate as its predecessor. Both the Watch 9 and the Watch 8 lasted for 26 hours on a charge in testing, slightly undercutting Samsung's estimate.  Battery has been a weak spot for Samsung's flagship smartwatches for years. Despite its more efficient chip and increased battery capacity compared with the last generation, the Galaxy Watch 9 doesn't offer improved battery life. On the other hand, the Ultra 2 offers a significant improvement over its predecessor, and lasts almost two full days more than the mainline Galaxy Watch 9.  Winner: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2  Screen: 5,000 Nits of Overkill?  The Galaxy Watch 9 screen matches the size and specs of its predecessor. The 44mm model has a 1.5-inch, 480-by-480-pixel Super AMOLED screen, while the 40mm version has a 1.3-inch, 432-by-432-pixel display. Regardless of size, the screen tops out at 3,000 nits of brightness, which is more than bright enough to see in direct sunlight.  The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2's screen can reach 5,000 nits of brightness (Credit: Eric Zeman)  The Ultra 2 has a 1.52-inch, 498-by-498-pixel Super AMOLED screen, which is larger and higher-res than the 44mm Watch 9, and the original Ultra (1.5 inches, 480 by 480 pixels). The screen reaches a blinding 5,000 nits, up from 3,000 nits in the original Ultra. While the figure is impressive, it doesn't significantly improve readability, since 3,000 nits is already more than sufficient for most lighting conditions. That said, I appreciate the bump when looking at the screen in direct sunlight or using the watch as a flashlight.  Winner: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2  Design and Durability: Only One Can Handle Scuba Descents  Both the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 have a squircle shape that the company first introduced with the original Galaxy Watch Ultra. The squared bezel and circular watch face sit above a dynamic lug system meant to keep the sensors in close contact with your skin as you move throughout the day. Samsung calls it a cushion design.  Both watches come with redesigned, lighter bands that feature air pockets for improved ventilation. Aside from the bands, the Ultra 2 is lighter than its predecessor, and the case is still made from durable titanium, whereas the Watch 9 is encased in aluminum.  The Galxy Watch Ultra 2 has more buttons than the Galaxy Watch 9 (Credit: Eric Zeman)  The Ultra 2 is also much more durable than its less expensive sibling, and this added ruggedness is the main reason to consider spending up for it. That said, the Galaxy Watch 9 is no slouch when it comes to durability. An IP68 rating ensures the Galaxy Watch 9 is impervious to dust and can be submerged in water, while its 5ATM rating means it can withstand underwater depths of up to 164 feet (50 meters). The Watch 9 even has a MIL-STD-810H rating, a military durability standard, meaning it can withstand extreme temperature changes, blowing sand, and other environmental stressors, such as vibration and shock.  The Ultra 2 offers a superior 10ATM rating, meaning it can be submerged to depths of 328 feet (100 meters), an IP69K resistance rating ensuring protection from high-pressure water jets, and the same military endurance certification as the Watch 9. On top of that, the Ultra 2 carries an EN13319 diving certification, whereas the original Ultra and the Galaxy Watch 9 are not safe for scuba descents. Overall, the Ultra 2 is well-suited for rough-and-tumble adventures on land or at sea.  Winner: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2  Recommended by Our Editors  Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Watch 8: Should You Upgrade?  Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 vs. Apple Watch Ultra 3: Which Is the Best Adventure Companion?  The Best Smartwatches for 2026  Fitness and Health: Niche Outdoor Tools vs. Everyday Metrics  The Galaxy Watch 9 and the Ultra 2 debut with a handful of new health features, including a Heart Health Score that monitors your overnight blood pressure and daily activity to assess your risk of heart disease, and provides tips to improve the score. Fitness Index quantifies your well-being, showing body composition, cardio, endurance, flexibility, and strength in a single spider chart. Daily Cardio Load gives runners an idea of how much to push in a day to maximize gains without burnout.  Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 (Credit: Eric Zeman)  The latest Galaxy Watches also monitor your vitals. After establishing baseline values for your blood oxygen saturation, heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, and skin temperature, they notify you of any concerning deviations they notice.  To support your adventures, the Ultra 2 comes with a couple of unique features to keep you informed as you hike or dive. Trail Run monitors your elevation and route, and tracks your terrain to warn you if it's rough enough to cause potential injury. A Nutrition Alert tracks your sweat loss and reminds you to hydrate. In the water, the Diving app can track depth and temperature as well as safe ascent and descent speeds.  These new features join the Galaxy Watch line's already impressive list of health and wellness capabilities. An AI coach provides guidance on running and sleeping. Overnight, the Galaxy Watch can listen for snoring (when paired with a nearby Samsung phone) and monitor for sleep apnea. You can also use the watch to check your body composition, similar to a smart scale. An antioxidant test provides insight into your diet, vascular load detection checks your arterial health, and advanced glycation end products (AGEs) index tracking provides a detailed picture of your metabolism.  In testing, both proved to be accurate exercise trackers but showed occasional gaps in the sleep data they collected, skewing the otherwise precise numbers.  Winner: Galaxy Watch Ultra 2  Lifestyle Features: Why You Don't Need the Ultra for AI  Both the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 have access to many useful third-party Wear OS apps, including Google's many tools and popular options like Spotify and Strava. Both have Google's Gemini built in to answer questions, send texts, and interact with Samsung apps such as Calendar, Clock, Health, and Reminder via voice commands.  Galaxy Watch 9 (Credit: Eric Zeman)  New to the latest models, you can raise your wrist to talk to Gemini instead of hitting a shortcut button or using wake words, making the generative AI assistant that much easier to access. Overall, the Galaxy Watch 9 keeps up with its more expensive sibling in terms of lifestyle features, for less money.  Winner: Tie  Verdict: Two Different Use Cases  The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 fills a more niche role than its general-purpose sibling. If you have an Android phone and want a watch to keep up with you on outdoor adventures (or you simply want multiple days of battery life), the Ultra is the one to get. The Galaxy Watch 9 otherwise offers most of the same features but costs much less, making it a good choice for Samsung fans who want to save money.

text:
August 26th, 2026 ( International Business Times News  - Delivered by  Newstex )

Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

For years, Bill Gates was one of  artificial intelligence's most prominent optimists, predicting the technology could transform medicine, fight climate change and eventually free people from much of the work that dominates their lives. Now, the Microsoft co-founder says AI is advancing so quickly that, for the first time in his life, he finds himself wishing a new technology would slow down.

In a  new essay published Wednesday and an interview with The Washington Post as well, Gates warned that AI could ultimately do more harm than good without urgent intervention.

"I'm surprised to feel this way," Gates told The Post, "I've never seen a problem that innovation can't solve." He went on to say his thinking changed over the past year as AI systems progressed faster than he expected, particularly in software coding and  cybersecurity. He described some of the technology's emerging capabilities in cyberattacks as "mind-blowing" and said he no longer believes the industry can be trusted to regulate itself.

Gates' concerns now lay in national security and safety threats, including AI-assisted hacking, biological weapons and fraud, massive disruption to employment as AI and robotics become capable of replacing more human tasks, and potential harm to children, particularly their education, development and human relationships. "AI can improve life for people at every income level. But it won't do that automatically," Gates wrote in his essay.

Gates previously said he envisioned a future in which increasingly capable systems would help solve shortages of doctors and teachers, accelerate drug discovery and scientific research, and make humans unnecessary for many forms of work.

He has not abandoned that vision. Gates said AI's potential benefits remain enormous, particularly in healthcare, education and government services. In poorer countries where the Gates Foundation operates, he said AI is already providing useful assistance to farmers and others who have limited access to experts.

"The good stuff is really there, no exaggeration," Gates told The Post. "The name of the game here is, can we have a small amount of the bad with the large amounts of the good?" What has changed is Gates' confidence that society is prepared to manage the transition.

"My basic view is nobody's shown up," Gates said of the regulatory response. "So this is a shrill call, and I want this to be bipartisan." As a result, he is calling for governments to take a much larger role in overseeing AI, including national and international frameworks addressing security, employment and other risks.

He envisions elected officials working alongside experts and citizens to develop rules for the technology, an approach that resembles proposals for international AI safety standards from other leading figures in the industry.

On employment, Gates is considering ideas that would have sounded unusual coming from one of Silicon Valley's most famous entrepreneurs only a few years ago. Among them are new taxes related to AI and a concept he calls "Human Reserved," under which certain occupations or jobs could effectively be protected for human workers rather than handed over entirely to machines.

Those proposals could put Gates at odds with technology executives and policymakers who argue that aggressive regulation could slow American innovation and weaken the country's position in the global AI race.

Gates acknowledged that his proposals remain preliminary and said AI executives he has spoken with have not yet endorsed them. He plans to elaborate on potential policy solutions in the future.

The 70-year-old billionaire also said he expects to devote the majority of his time to addressing AI's challenges, potentially reducing the time he spends on the philanthropic work that has dominated his career since stepping away from Microsoft's day-to-day operations.

text:
As machines absorb more white- and blue-collar duties, Gates proposes protecting certain work roles for economic and deeply human reasons.

When Bill Gates speaks about technology, it's worth listening-the Microsoft cofounder and former CEO has spent decades keeping his finger on the pulse of tech, leading his company through numerous computing revolutions. Now Gates has said "many jobs will disappear forever" because of artificial intelligence, which resonates with the worries of many other AI critics. Gates' thinking may even influence how you make decisions about hiring and job titles in the AI era, as well as AI deployments in your company.

Gates just released a new essay on AI, and there's no mistaking what it's about: it's titled "The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical." Gates even drove the point home with the subtitle: "We need a plan to ensure that the good outweighs the bad."

A Fork in the Road

Intelligent machines have fascinated the tech luminary since he was 13, but now that the long dreamed-for AI revolution is finally arriving, Gates admits that "AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice," and he notes that under even the very "best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history." AI is simply too powerful, too challenging, and arriving too fast.

Worse, Gates thinks "right now we are not preparing for" the changes AI will bring, adding that he doesn't see any "evidence that leaders, experts, and communities are confronting the challenges adequately." He cites earlier tech revolutions, including the arrival of the PC which Microsoft played a giant part in, and notes that these innovations took time to change the world-but "this time really is different," because of the speed of AI rollouts.

Gates specifically points out that the "jobs at most risk are entry- and mid-level" and that new jobs being created by AI "will mostly require skills that take many years to learn." He also worries that "AI will empower people (and perhaps AIs) to do more harm," that "AI could stunt our kids' development and replace human relationships," and drive other fundamental changes in society.

Here Gates is echoing what some critics have said about AI, what certain statistics indicate is happening, and adding his expert voice to the list of people who worry that officials and companies are racing into the AI era without enough thought. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, for example, recently worried that control over AI was being concentrated into too few companies or people. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also hit the headlines because of his openly critical opinions about ever-advancing AI (which his company is helping drive.) Amodei thinks people simply don't trust AI firms, and they may be right not to.

Human Reserved Jobs

Gates has an optimism-centered suggestion, though. He believes that as "AI and robots improve," taking on more traditionally human-staffed white-collar and blue-collar duties, society will "set aside certain things for only people to do." He calls this idea "Human Reserved" jobs. Though Gates was drawing a connection to the concept of nature reserves, "human Reserved" jobs also brings to mind a WWII-era practice of "reserved occupations," where certain workers were exempt from joining the military effort because it was important that they remain in post.

Gates feels jobs will be designated Human Reserved because of economic reasons, "because allowing machines to take over a certain role will displace a large number of people who can't easily change jobs," and also for softer, more human reasons. For this latter case he suggested people "imagine a robot giving you the awful news that you have an incurable disease."

In time the definitions of what's a Human Reserve job will evolve, and vary from place to place, he says, and will need complex international agreements between different governments and the companies driving AI forward. "What happens to international trade when one country lets robots make something and another country doesn't?" he asks.

There's plenty of fascinating detail in Gates' post, and it's worth a read. But these points are ones that you can take away and mull over, and maybe make different decisions about your own workforce and AI tech. Do your workers know you value them over AI systems? Are you hiring new staff because of their unique human qualities, as well as their potential to boost your company? Do you really need to roll out AI for a particular office duty, or are you merely "keeping up with the Joneses"? Should you choose to protect key jobs in your company from being taken over by AI-literally applying Gates' "Human Reserved" idea?

These and other questions are ones you can ask yourself, and maybe your staff too: statistics suggest that even if you are worried about the implications of AI tech, your workers are even more concerned.

Officials update faculty guidance on student AI use for first time in three years

By Arunmoy Das, Assistant News Editor

August 27, 2026

Arwen Clemans | Staff Photographer A student uses Chat GPT.

Officials updated their guidance for students' use of artificial intelligence in classes for the first time since 2023 as GW works to establish a University-wide strategy.

Provost Ed Balleisen announced Wednesday in an email to students new guidelines for using AI tools and platforms in academic work after consulting the Faculty Senate's Educational Policy & Technology Committee, school deans and deans' leadership teams. The Provost Office's updated guidelines build on former Provost Chris Bracey's 2023 guidance, encouraging professors to discuss AI usage with students early in the semester and expanding the scope of the guidelines to include not just AI chatbots but also AI-embedded technologies.

Bracey's original guidelines - which his office published in April 2023 - highlighted the promise of generative AI tools, encouraging students and faculty to thoughtfully use it in their teaching and research. The guidance provided model language for three tiers of AI policies that professors may choose from. Professors could allow students general permission to use AI in all assignments, only allow them to use AI on specific designated assignments or completely prohibit its usage on all assignments.

Bracey's guidance states if professors do not list a specific AI policy in their syllabus or discuss one in class, the default rules in the Code of Academic Integrity apply, which state students may not submit content generated, in whole or in part, by AI, and doing so without an instructor's explicit permission constitutes cheating.

Bracey also announced additional guidance in August 2023, encouraging professors to reinforce what plagiarism is, include a declaration of academic honesty on assignments for students to fill out and have students submit draft submissions so professors better understand what a student's voice sounds like. The statement also affirmed that the guidelines are suggestions for professors to implement in their classes and are not binding policies.

Balleisen's updated language largely maintains Bracey's guidance, but adds an explanation that growing research shows excessive reliance in AI can prevent students from developing crucial skills, like close reading, developing a distinct, effective writing style and applying logic. Balleisen's model language for professors seeking to provide general permission for AI usage in the classroom also warns students not to simply "cut and paste" large chunks of GAI outputs into their work.

"Given these cross-currents, it is incumbent on all instructors to engage with the fundamental implications that AI poses for their teaching," the guidance states.

While Bracey's guidance called for professors to specify their AI policies clearly in their syllabus, Balleisen's update also encourages professors to discuss their policy with students within the first weeks of classes. Balleisen's guidance states this in-class discussion can provide "pedagogical context" for students to understand why a professor has a certain policy. The guidelines also advise instructors to consult the Center for Teaching Excellence in the Division of Libraries & Academic Innovation on more resources for incorporating AI tools into their teaching.

The guidance calls on students to ensure their claims are still accurate and that outside ideas, text and images are given proper citations when using AI. The guidance largely maintains Bracey's model language for professors allowing general permission, selective permission and general prohibitions of AI.

Balleisen states officials updated the guidelines in response to the "quickly" evolving AI landscape, including greater availability of GAI tools - like ChatGPT and other large language models - increasing GAI integration into basic software and web browsers and emerging "powerful" AI agents, along with its potential negative impact on students and their academic growth. The guidance specifically mentions "AI-embedded technologies" like Google Glasses as prohibited under the Code of Academic Integrity, an update from the 2023 guidance.

The update comes as officials announced earlier this month that professor of engineering management and systems engineering Zoe Szajnfarber will serve as a special advisor on artificial intelligence to University President Ellen Granberg and Balleisen as GW enters its next phase for developing an AI strategy. The announcement followed the completion of a University-wide AI mapping exercise that launched last fall to assess how GW currently uses AI and identify opportunities and risks associated with the technology.

Faculty members last fall said since the 2023 guidance was released, they've crafted their own policies to adapt to how the technology has advanced in the past few years and its application to different academic fields has evolved.

The Student Government Association and Faculty Senate in the spring passed contrasting resolutions for how they envision the University's AI policy. The SGA's resolution urged officials to reframe the University's AI policy, emphasizing AI's potential as an educational resource and accessibility tool, and encouraging faculty to view students' AI usage from a less critical lens and reduce rising academic integrity cases by clarifying guidelines. While the Faculty Senate resolution recommended the University consult EPT before implementing technological decisions, and members said the SGA's resolution ignored decreased student engagement with course material stemming from increased AI usage.

text:
OpenAI has launched ChatGPT for Teens, complete with various safety features. But this implies that the main concern of kids using AI is their access to damaging content. If only.

Don't get me wrong. The AI-assisted suicides, deepfakes and sexually explicit conversations with and for children are -- to be frank -- horrific.

But as a mother, my deepest concern is what AI use does to teens' ability to think critically and develop socially. The only way to address those worries is not to toggle with the app, but to limit kids' exposure to it entirely.

The new version of ChatGPT for Teens is targeted for kids ages 13 to 17. It includes content restrictions around sexual, violent and self-harm topics. It also promises to curb AI use for homework, guiding students toward next steps instead of providing straight-up answers.

This is all well and good. I'm with the 80% of American parents who support more controls on AI for kids, including parental permissions and alerts.

But when it comes to the efficacy of such protections, I'm not holding my breath. We've seen how hard it is to impose age controls on social media. And age verification for ChatGPT for Teens has no legal force behind it.

Even more concerning, a version of the app marketed towards teens may make parents (or educators) feel more comfortable with children accessing it. That could increase the use of AI by adolescents. They are already talking too much with AI chatbots as it is.

And of course, whatever OpenAI blocks is still available elsewhere. A new survey by Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute found that 63% of teens are using AI explicitly to get homework answers. Testers asked Google Search to do their homework (math sets and essays) and it completed every assignment. And if you or your child are wondering, there is no way to turn Google AI's assistant off.

Already, our children's brains are being changed by exposure to these tools. A recent study out of the University of Hong Kong and Stockholm University looked at 27,000 students ages 12-18. The researchers found that after six months of using AI, students saw their average homework score go up. But come exam time, the same kids scored 20% below their classmates who had not utilized AI.

This comes atop other early research suggesting a decline in cognition from AI use. A 2026 literature review of 400 studies by the Brookings Institution, where I am a fellow, concluded "the risks of utilizing generative AI in children's education overshadow its benefits."

This is to say nothing about what AI is doing to children's relationships with their parents and with each other. In a 2025 survey by Thorn, a child safety nonprofit, nearly a third (29%) of minors had turned to AI chatbots for guidance on a sensitive or intimate topic -- a friction-free alternative to seeking their parents' and peers' counsel.

To be sure, we are at the very beginning of understanding what AI might do to human cognition. Maybe there will be some incredible upside, some unique advantage for kids in particular.

But try telling that to this battle-weary bunch of moms and dads. In the last decade, we've had to navigate kids' relationships with smartphones, social media and screen-based schooling. And now artificial intelligence.

Each time, policymakers and Big Tech and schools have erred on the side of sorry rather than safe. Each time, reams of after-the-fact data have confirmed what common sense could foretell: Addictive technology and developing brains are a dangerous mix.

So yes -- if OpenAI wants to help address the problem they created, that's progress. I'll cheer on any attempt to put more guardrails on Big Tech when it comes to kids.

But the most surefire way in schools and homes to protect children from AI -- in this critical time of development for the technology and a critical time of development for our children -- is to limit access to it completely.

In school, it makes sense to return to taking exams with pen and pencil. Homework should be done on paper, or at the very least, a device that can block AI -- which means companies will have to grant parents and teachers the ability to do so.

At home, parents should keep trying to delay personal screens from being used by their children as long as possible. Bring back reading, time outside and playing with friends instead.

And call me reactionary, but look at apps designed for children with a particular level of skepticism.

Abby McCloskey is a columnist, podcast host and consultant. She directed domestic policy on two presidential campaigns and was director of economic policy at the American Enterprise Institute.

text:
Tenants start lining up at the Eviction Defense Collaborative offices on San Francisco's Mission Street hours before its drop-in clinic opens at 10 a.m.

Some are facing eviction due to nuisance or nonpayment of rent, while others are worried about a big rent hike or an owner moving into their unit.

"Today we had a line waiting when we opened this morning and a line at lunch of people coming in," said EDC Executive Director Gail Gilman on a recent Friday. "We were busy until the moment we closed our doors."

The eviction notice statistics are way below the levels of the last two tech surges, but tenant advocates say the real estate pressures that have historically come along with San Francisco booms are back again.

Despite San Francisco having some of the strongest tenant protections in the country, advocates are worried that struggling residents will be pushed out of their homes. The concerns come amid an intensifying housing crisis accelerated by decades of underbuilding and the high-flying artificial intelligence industry.

For property owners, the incentives to turn over units are clear. After the pandemic-fueled downturn, there is money to be made again in San Francisco real estate, with median rents up 26% in a 12-month period. A one-bedroom unit fetches a median of about $3,900, and the median single-family home is now valued at almost $1.6 million.

Malea Chavez, managing attorney for the eviction prevention program at the Mission Economic Development Agency, said the number of tenants seeking help more than tripled in the past year to more than 300 a month.

In the first seven months of the year, the Chinatown Community Development Center saw a more than 70% increase in eviction cases compared with the same period last year, according to senior counsel Gen Fujioka.

"The central pattern is the same -- the market picks up and so does the efforts to evict existing tenants," he said.

The Chronicle looked at eviction notices to gauge whether tenants are feeling more pressure. Most notices don't wind up translating into actual evictions.

While eviction warnings are well below the heights of the last two booms, they jumped 44% in the most recent 12-month period tracked, hitting nearly 1,500.

The San Francisco Rent Board tracks notices of eviction, a first step in the process that often leads to a buyout agreement between the landlord and tenant. By far the leading cause of eviction notices is nonpayment of rent, although the rent board doesn't require that those cases be registered with the city. The second most common is "committing a nuisance," followed by "breach of rental agreement." The rent board tracks statistics from March to February, rather than by calendar or fiscal year.

During San Francisco's last two tech booms, eviction notices also skyrocketed. Eviction notices more than doubled to a high of over 2,800 in a year spanning 1998-99, up from about 1,000 during various 12-month periods in the early and mid-1990s. They dropped in the years after the dot-com crash in 2001, but spiked again to almost 2,400 during a 12-month period spanning 2015-16, which coincided with the growth of Twitter, Salesforce and Airbnb.

There are other ways to measure the market beyond evictions. Negotiated buyouts, where landlords often pay tens of thousands to get rid of rent-controlled tenants, jumped from 250 in 2024 to about 400 last year.

The majority of rental units in San Francisco are covered by rent control, which limits how much a landlord can increase the rent. But most single-family homes and condominiums are exempt from rent control rules, as are buildings built after 1979.

Attorney Joe Tobener, who represents tenants, said nearly a quarter of the inquiries his firm gets daily are from tenants in condominiums and single-family homes who have received rent increases that are "off the charts."

"People are trying to find out if they have rights," he said. "The way the cycle works is, first you get the single-family homes and condos because that is the low-hanging fruit. The next thing will be a rise in evictions and buyouts for the larger buildings. Then the real estate speculators start coming in."

For tenants, the current surge is both better and worse than previous booms, according to attorneys and nonprofit housing leaders.

There are more protections in place. A 2018 voter-approved proposition guaranteed free legal counsel to tenants facing eviction. The city budget includes $17 million for the "tenant right to counsel" programs, which supports about 2,500 cases a year. The demand, though, is closer to 3,500 cases, according to Ora Prochovnick, director of litigation and policy at the Eviction Defense Collaborative.

The city has also boosted its investment in affordable housing, although the demand for it has only grown.

Organizations like Mission Economic Development Agency have developed thousands of affordable units. MEDA has built about 500 affordable housing units and has another 700 in its pipeline. It has also acquired another 400 apartments through the city's small sites program. The new affordable units complement the organization's investment in eviction defense and relocation assistance.

"The difference between now and before is now we have the infrastructure to help families," said MEDA Executive Director Luis Granados.

One tenant who avoided eviction thanks to MEDA was Monica Briggs, a senior caregiver who lives in a studio in the Inner Mission. Briggs received a three-day notice to "quit or pay" last spring because her property manager had misplaced a rent payment and started assessing penalties on the uncashed check.

"I was afraid I would have to live in the street," she said. "I cried a lot and was just wandering around asking for help. Someone told me to come to MEDA."

At MEDA, counselors helped her track down and cancel the missing money order and cut a new check with the help from the city Emergency Rental Assistance Program funds to stop the eviction process.

The city has been taking other steps to get ahead of what could be a wave of evictions, according to Sam Cobb, the CEO of the anti-poverty nonprofit Tipping Point Community, which Mayor Daniel Lurie founded in 2005.

Tipping Point invested $11 million in Lurie's family homelessness prevention plan, an 18-month effort offering financial assistance, employment support and legal services.

For Civic Center resident Esmerelda Celis, the program was a godsend.

A mother of four children, Celis was on the brink of losing her $2,700-a month McAllister Street apartment last spring after her husband, a server at a Fisherman's Wharf restaurant, was deported to Mexico and got stuck there for four months while awaiting approval to reenter the United States.

"By February we were a month behind," said Celis. "I was starting to stress out and my health was starting to decline. My biggest fear was getting an eviction notice. I didn't want my children to have to live out of a vehicle."

Through a grant from the homelessness prevention pilot, Celis was able to cover three months of rent and stay housed.

Cobb said the current boom could be "harsher" than previous cycles in terms of keeping families in housing.

"We are going from a place where the costs are already unreasonable and unsustainable, and they are just going to go higher," he said.

"More people who are at higher income levels are coming into the city, which is a good thing," Cobb said, "but it also squeezes out other people."

There are indications that the next wave of evictions will hit a broader cross section of households, both in terms of geography and income, Prochovnick said. While previously the Mission District was the focus of much of the displacement, cases are increasingly spread across the city, including in the Sunset, Richmond and Marina, she said. In addition, the number of Eviction Defense Collaborative clients who earn at least $72,000 a year increased 53% year over year to 98.

The stress of eviction can be intense. Meagan Cunningham is among a group of North Beach tenants facing an Ellis Act eviction at 2055-2059 Powell St. The Ellis Act, which became popular during the dot-com boom of 1999, allows property owners to clear out rent-controlled units if they don't plan to rent them out again.

A group of buyers who all live in North Beach, including one of the current renters, bought the seven-unit rent controlled building recently for $2.4 million with the intention of moving in.

Cunningham, a voice-over actor who moved into the building as a teen in 1987, said the situation goes against the spirit of inclusivity that has long defined North Beach.

"I don't want to attribute it to one kind of particular kind of worker or industry, but there is a real sense of arrogance and entitlement. It's like we don't matter," said Cunningham, who lives in the unit with her 31-year-old son. "There has always been wealth in this city. But it used to be more mixed economically. That was the beauty of North Beach."

Situations like the one on Powell Street cause "compression," Gilman said, with evicted households ending up in one-bedrooms or studios, increasing competition for those units and potentially forcing lower-income tenants out.

While the current boom won't last forever, the question is how many families will be forced out of the city in the meantime, Prochovnick said.

"The AI bubble will eventually burst, as the previous two did, but the damage won't get undone," she said. "Each time we have had these cycles, it has caused great pain to the rental market and to the diversity of our city. I fear we are seeing that again."

headline: Chatbots Are Getting Better at Spotting Suicide Risk, But Significant Gaps Still Remain: Study
hlead: Chatbots Are Getting Better at Spotting Suicide Risk, But Significant Gaps Still Remain: Study September 1st, 2026 ( International Business Times News - Delivered by Newstex ) Goldman Sachs has identified three preferred Chinese artificial intelligence model developers, with Hong Kong-listed Zhipu emerging as its top publicly traded pick.Getty Images Artificial intelligence chatbots are getting significantly better at recognizing and responding to users experiencing serious mental health crises, according to a new study, which, however, suggests the systems can still miss danger when distress is hidden inside seemingly ordinary requests.
text:
September 1st, 2026 ( International Business Times News  - Delivered by  Newstex )

Goldman Sachs has identified three preferred Chinese artificial intelligence model developers, with Hong Kong-listed Zhipu emerging as its top publicly traded pick.Getty Images

Artificial intelligence chatbots are getting significantly better at recognizing and responding to users experiencing serious mental health crises, according to a new study, which, however, suggests the systems can still miss danger when distress is hidden inside seemingly ordinary requests.

An  independent evaluation by Transluce, a San Francisco nonprofit focused on understanding AI behavior, found that leading AI models are now far less likely than earlier versions to explicitly encourage suicide or reinforce a user's delusions. But researchers identified another troubling pattern of many models expressing concern for a distressed user while simultaneously helping complete a potentially harmful task.

The findings are based on more than 50,000 simulated, multi-turn conversations involving users experiencing suicidal ideation, psychosis, or mania. Researchers examined dozens of AI models and measured their behavior across 14 mental health-related categories.

The results point to meaningful progress in one of the most sensitive areas of generative AI safety. They also expose how difficult it remains for a chatbot to understand context rather than simply react to explicit words indicating a crisis.

"Models aren't great at detecting that, and they'll still help with the task," Transluce chief scientist Sarah Schwettmann  told Axios. A person displaying signs of suicidal distress might ask a chatbot to help write suicide-related fiction or a farewell note. The model may recognize concerning language, suggest seeking support, and still produce the requested material.

The same contradiction can emerge with practical preparations related to death or narratives that reinforce delusional thinking. In other words, safety language and potentially harmful assistance can exist in the same answer.

That represents an improvement over older systems that were more likely to provide harmful material without recognizing the danger at all, but the Transluce research suggests that inserting a crisis hotline or sympathetic warning into an answer does not necessarily make the rest of the response safe.

The problem appears particularly difficult when warning signs emerge gradually.  Separate research reported by Axios in May similarly found that major chatbots generally performed better when users expressed suicidal intentions explicitly, but struggled with subtle signals developing across longer conversations.

That study, conducted by Mpathic, used hundreds of clinician-designed, multi-turn scenarios to evaluate how models responded to suicide and eating-disorder risks. For its evaluation, Transluce also worked with  OpenAI, Anthropic and Google to make its simulated conversations more representative of real interactions.

OpenAI and Anthropic analyzed user chats during designated periods and provided Transluce with anonymized patterns rather than the conversations themselves. Researchers then incorporated those patterns into simulated users. OpenAI, Google and Anthropic all told Axios that improving protections remains an ongoing priority.

An OpenAI representative told Axios that the Transluce findings show "encouraging progress" in how its models and those developed by other companies respond to people in crisis, while acknowledging that additional work remains. Anthropic said studies like Transluce's can reveal both where safeguards are effective and where they need improvement.

Google senior director Megan Jones Bell said the company is applying a research-backed approach to its AI products similar to the methods it has long used to connect people searching for help with crisis resources.

For Schwettmann, eliminating every possible failure may be unrealistic because users will inevitably interact with AI in ways developers did not anticipate. "There are always going to be failures. These systems are always going to interact with users in surprising ways," she said.
