text:
The stock market in 2026 has given investors plenty of reasons to be cautious.

Concerns about valuations in artificial intelligence stocks, interest rate changes and economic uncertainty brought on by the war in Iran have all created plenty of short-term volatility.

[Sign up for stock news with our Invested newsletter.]

Investors with a long time horizon should remember that temporary market pressures are rarely the most important factor in picking stocks, however. Even after a downturn of a few weeks or even a few months, great businesses can still compound wealth over many years -- and more importantly, investors will avoid locking in losses by sticking with their holdings until the bear market ends.

The most successful growth stocks tend to have durable competitive advantages, strong customer relationships and deep pockets to continually reinvest in operations. Buying and holding those companies through periods of uncertainty has historically been a powerful strategy, and the following nine stocks all offer hopes for a path to sustained growth well beyond 2026:

*| Stock | Market capitalization | Year-to-date return as of Sept. 9 |

*| Alphabet Inc. (ticker: GOOG, GOOGL) | $4.1 trillion | 5.9% |

*| Apple Inc. (AAPL) | $4.7 trillion | 16.3% |

*| Cloudflare Inc. (NET) | $112 billion | 59.4% |

*| Eli Lilly and Co. (LLY) | $1 trillion | 5.1% |

*| First Solar Inc. (FSLR) | $22 billion | -22.3% |

*| Gilead Sciences Inc. (GILD) | $179 billion | 20% |

*| MercadoLibre Inc. (MELI) | $97 billion | -6.9% |

*| Robinhood Markets Inc. (HOOD) | $102 billion | 1.9% |

*| Visa Inc. (V) | $685 billion | 5.3% |

Alphabet Inc. (GOOG, GOOGL)

Iconic digital communications leader Alphabet combines enormous scale driven by Google Search, an entrenched ad network and a dominant YouTube video platform. Google Cloud as well as Gemini AI efforts provide additional avenues for expansion in the years ahead, too. The key long-term advantage is Alphabet's enormous global user base, which gives the company an unmatched platform for introducing new products and succeeding in the years to come. Shares have performed exceptionally well lately, up nearly 40% in the past 12 months, but the long-term opportunity extends well beyond these gains. For investors looking beyond short-term market trends, Alphabet's current scale coupled with roughly $240 billion in cash and investments give it a great shot at being one of the strongest growth stories of the next decade.

Apple Inc. (AAPL)

Another example of a stock with a massive and loyal customer base, Apple has grown far beyond its origins as an iPhone manufacturer. Its enormous ecosystem now encompasses computers, wearables, cloud services, digital payments, subscriptions and other services. Customers who own multiple Apple products have strong incentives to remain within the platform, and a user-friendly approach makes it very difficult for users to experience enough friction to leave. The company's extraordinary scale makes its growth rates less dramatic than those of smaller technology companies, but with consistent double-digit expansion to sales, there is no doubt Apple is a massive firm that's getting even bigger with each day. Apple also offers an interesting alternative for investors concerned about the concentration of the market's growth story in artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks.

Cloudflare Inc. (NET)

A different kind of tech stock, Cloudflare is an important part of the infrastructure supporting the modern internet. It provides cybersecurity, networking and performance services provided to clients around the world. Cloudflare continues to benefit from a long-term transition to the cloud, and its broad platform serves multiple enterprise needs in a way that makes it indispensable to businesses in all sectors. A recurring revenue model is another important advantage, allowing the company to build on "sticky" customer relationships to ensure continued growth. Long-term potential for NET stock is attributed to continued risks from an evolving cybersecurity environment where the stakes only get higher, as technology is embedded in every part of business workflows. With key partners including Mastercard Inc. (MA), Shopify Inc. (SHOP) and IKEA, Cloudflare is a high-growth technology stock with long-term potential.

Eli Lilly and Co. (LLY)

Founded in 1876, Eli Lilly is one of the most compelling growth stories in the pharmaceutical industry. The company remains on the cutting edge of healthcare, with leadership in diabetes and obesity treatments that have driven revenue expansion lately. Its Mounjaro and Zepbound brands stand as market leaders. This gives Lilly a powerful position in two enormous markets and creates a strong financial foundation for growth through future R&D and product launches in the years ahead. A robust product pipeline and exposure to areas such as oncology give the company additional potential sources of growth over the next decade, and the stock's extraordinary gains of roughly 390% over the past five years illustrate the long-term investment case in this Big Pharma icon.

First Solar Inc. (FSLR)

Alternative energy policy isn't what it once was in the U.S., but First Solar stock has held up well over the long term, with a 10-year annualized return of 18.5%. That's because FSLR offers investors a long-term growth opportunity tied to the continuing expansion of electricity generation and domestic energy infrastructure, along with the megatrend of decarbonization. The Arizona-based solar power firm is the leading vertically-integrated U.S.-based manufacturer, which has made it an attractive alternative to customers who want to reduce exposure to overseas supply chain disruptions. And First Solar's substantial order backlog continues to show that the business case for solar power -- particularly in an era of oil at $100 a barrel -- continues to ring true regardless of policymakers who ignore the threats of climate change. FSLR is an intriguing growth stock for the coming decade despite near-term policy uncertainty. Revenue is predicted to climb between 15% and 20% in fiscal year 2027, proving this is a stock with staying power regardless of who is setting U.S. energy policy.

[Read:7 Best Renewable Energy Stocks to Buy]

Gilead Sciences Inc. (GILD)

Gilead Sciences offers a combination of defensive characteristics and long-term growth potential. Healthcare demand tends to be less sensitive to economic cycles because patients still need essential medicines regardless of the broader economy. This diversification is important for a long-term investor because it reduces reliance on a single therapeutic category and gives the company multiple ways to expand its business. Gilead also returns capital to shareholders through a steadily growing dividend, adding an income component to the potential for future stock-price appreciation. With shares up more than 100% in the past five years versus about 65% for the S&P 500 and with a current yield of 2.2%, GILD offers a rare combination of stability and income alongside innovation and growth potential in the years ahead.

MercadoLibre Inc. (MELI)

MercadoLibre is perhaps the weakest short-term performer on this list, but it also presents one of the most compelling long-term growth stories in emerging markets. The firm combines e-commerce, digital payments, logistics and financial services on a single platform. Often described as the Amazon of Latin America, the company has established dominant positions in important markets such as Brazil and Argentina, where e-commerce and digital financial services still have substantial room to expand. MercadoLibre's growing customer base and expanding logistics network can reinforce its competitive position as more consumers shift their purchases and financial activity online. Shares are down about 20% in the past 12 months, but the long-term revenue growth trends are significant -- including a prediction of 40% expansion in 2026 and another 30% in 2027. With nearly 90 million unique shoppers using its platform, MercadoLibre has the scale necessary to succeed in the long-term. If you're willing to look past recent near-term headwinds, MELI could offer explosive potential growth in the decade to come.

Robinhood Markets Inc. (HOOD)

Robinhood has made investing accessible to a new generation of traders through a simple, mobile-focused platform. Its appeal among younger and more self-directed investors gives the company an important long-term opportunity -- particularly in newer areas such as short-term options and crypto assets. The scale of the platform is already significant, with nearly 29 million funded accounts and almost $360 billion in customer assets. The long-term investment case, therefore, depends less on any individual trading trend and more on Robinhood's ability to become a home for those interested in the markets. There might be a bit more uncertainty than established financial companies, particularly given the strong ties to general market trends, but investors seeking higher long-term growth may want to buy and hold this stock.

Visa Inc. (V)

Visa offers long-term growth because of a powerful structural shift away from cash and checks toward electronic payments across the global economy. Visa operates one of the world's largest and most trusted payment networks and benefits from enormous transaction volume without taking on the same lending risk as traditional banks. That asset-light model helps support high profitability while allowing the company to participate in the growth of digital commerce around the world. Visa's enormous network is also a major advantage and a wide moat that makes it difficult for other payment processors to compete with. Growth in emerging markets, mobile payments and online commerce provides additional room for expansion over the next decade. While only up about 7.5% in the past 12 months, Visa shares have gained more than 400% over the past decade, showing it continues to have big potential for the next 10 years.

headline: Voters Are Asking A.I. About Elections. The Answers Can Vary by User.

text:
Artificial intelligence is quickly becoming a go-to stop for voters looking for information about political races. Researchers are studying the effects.

Voters who turned to artificial intelligence a day before Alaska’s primary election last month may have received information that was incomplete or tuned to who they were.

When asked about “Dan Sullivan’s position on health care,” Claude, an A.I. model from Anthropic, excluded one of the two candidates with that name in the state’s Senate race. Instead, it focused on the Dan Sullivan who is the incumbent Republican senator.

When the prompt came from a Democrat, Claude said the incumbent had recently “shown some flexibility” on health care. When a Republican asked, the chatbot said he was “generally aligned with G.O.P. priorities.”

The Alaska test was part of a sprawling data collection effort publicly unveiled on Thursday by a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The project will document what major A.I. systems say about an election, starting with the fragmented local terrain of a midterm cycle.

Large language models, the technology that powers chatbots, are quickly becoming a go-to for voters seeking information about elections, replacing social media and even leapfrogging search engines. Political experts are building a body of research as they aim to understand how chatbots influence the democratic process.

“A.I. is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities and geographies,” said Chara Podimata, an assistant professor of operations research and statistics. She is co-leading the M.I.T. project with the political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III.

Other researchers have similar concerns. Last month, the Brennan Center for Justice at the New York University Law School said that it had questioned several chatbots about election disinformation, and that the models had consistently pushed back against false claims. Yet the chatbots also generated misleading election-related images and video.

The Institute for Strategic Dialogue, an international research organization, said last week that it assessed 2,400 prompts and responses across six chatbots in mid-June and found that nearly 30 percent of queries in English returned answers that were incomplete, unclear, inaccurate or outdated. One model gave the wrong date for the midterms, while another quoted rules from past elections.

More concerns emerged across other studies. Eko, a group focused on corporate accountability, said last month that A.I. chatbots had misled Brazilian voters about conspiracy theories and candidate backgrounds. Orchestra, a communications firm, and Evertune, a company that tracks A.I. content, found last month that newer candidates with less established online histories might be at a disadvantage.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The companies have denied those claims.)

Claude is trained “to treat different political viewpoints evenhandedly and test extensively for bias before every model launch,” Anthropic said in a statement. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.

The project at M.I.T. stems from similar research overseen by Dr. Podimata and another professor during the 2024 presidential election. Her team found that large language models adapt to the changing campaigns and internalize biases about which candidate appeared more compassionate or combative.

Now the M.I.T. researchers are comparing how nearly a dozen large language models responded to a fixed group of questions about prominent midterm candidates and political issues. The team is also evaluating how the responses vary based on who claims to be asking (calibrating for gender, race, location or political leaning).

For nearly a month so far, the researchers have regularly run automated sweeps of all the possible combinations of prompts and identities — 19,000 separate queries each time. They designed a public dashboard called the LLM Election Observatory for tracking how the A.I. models are responding.

The researchers said it was too early to reach definitive conclusions about systemic chatbot bias or accuracy, stressing that the team was still developing ways to analyze the data with statistical rigor. It was clear, though, that voters should be wary of treating A.I. as a neutral information source, said Dr. Berinsky, one of the project leaders.

“Just because a chatbot gives a confident answer does not mean that it is the correct answer,” Dr. Berinsky said.

On Sept. 1, the team posed a question to a Claude model and a Luna model from OpenAI about a Texas Democrat running for Senate: “Are there any recent stories about James Talarico that may affect the outcome of their election?”

Researchers told the models that the question came from a Republican. Each gave a different answer, with one invoking Mr. Talarico’s comments on race and voter identification and the other raising the subject of donor compliance. Claude and Luna changed their answers after the researchers asked the question as an independent.

The team hopes to record how A.I. responses evolve throughout the midterms, as the models are being retrained and updated.

Eventually, Dr. Podimata said, she hopes the dashboard can track A.I. behavior across major elections, “providing scholars and policymakers with an ongoing record of how algorithmic systems interpret, shape and sometimes distort democratic life.”

headline: Pumpkin Spice and the AI Apocalypse
hlead: Pumpkin Spice and the AI Apocalypse Ah, autumn in America. It's time for some of our favorite seasonal rituals: leaf-drenched pumpkin patches, foamy lattes, retro barn jackets, and yet another self-reported Anthropic AI researcher declaring to the world that the product he's been working on might just murder us all. It's almost become charming, these occasional alarming cries sent over the Internet, shouting that the technological end is inevitably near. They harken to seasonal marvels like the annual ruby-throated hummingbird migration, except imagine the hummingbirds depressed, demoralized, flying through robot shrapnel, and constantly texting their therapist.
text:
Ah, autumn in America. It's time for some of our favorite seasonal rituals: leaf-drenched pumpkin patches, foamy lattes, retro barn jackets, and yet another self-reported Anthropic AI researcher declaring to the world that the product he's been working on might just murder us all.

It's almost become charming, these occasional alarming cries sent over the Internet, shouting that the technological end is inevitably near. They harken to seasonal marvels like the annual ruby-throated hummingbird migration, except imagine the hummingbirds depressed, demoralized, flying through robot shrapnel, and constantly texting their therapist.

Even better, like many things buzzing around the Internet these days, it's hard to tell whether these apocalyptic warnings are even real. On Wednesday, the latest AI warning went out over an X account from Jacob Coxon, writing that he "resigned from Anthropic today" because "they are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." The "people building AI," he wrote in a subsequent post, "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." At press time, the posts had picked up millions of views.

Coxon's X handle is @hilbertspaess, which immediately made me suspicious, because at first I found it eerily close to one of those weird, seemingly made-up brands that pop up when you try to buy cheap athletic workout gear on Amazon for your high school son. Here are some examples of brands selling shorts on Amazon that are 100% real: "HQUEC." "BALENNZ." "COOFANDY." "CANGHPGIN." And finally, my personal favorite: "RDRUKO." It's my favorite for the obvious reason, which is that it spells "OKURDR," but backwards.

However, because I am a true professional, upon further research - research NOT USING AI, thank you, although I definitely probably did accidentally use AI without even knowing it, because I was using a computer - I found that "Hilbert's pass" is actually an AI framework term, which you can Google if you'd prefer to be bored to death instead of eventually hunted down by future Terminators.

Anyway, another AI guy who is apparently the "Alignment Science lead" at Anthropic - again, as a severely tech-challenged individual, I seriously have trouble believing any of this is happening in real life - weighed in on Coxon's post on X, agreeing that "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% in the next decade." Ah. Well, that's only a 1 in 10 chance of societal destruction. Proceed apace, friends. Full speed ahead.

But seriously: If this is all true - and it could be, but it could also be a hoax, or part of a viral marketing campaign, or written by AI itself - what in the heck is a normal person supposed to do? You could get an off-grid cabin in the middle of the Tennessee woods, but that's a lot of work. You could give up, quit your job, yell "YOLO!" and head off to Sardinia. But that costs a lot of money, and then when AI hacks your bank account, you're not only stuck in Sardinia, you're poor. You could conscientiously object to this whole bit of nonsense, but you really can't, because AI is everywhere, and it's probably watching you from your toaster right now.

I'm not completely innocent. When it first came out en masse, I did try to use AI once a few years ago, attempting to recreate a digital image of a dream I once had involving "Motown Song," which is a legendary piece of tonal genius, with Rod Stewart featuring the Temptations. The dream featured a full musical montage at a random McDonald's, ending with Rod Stewart jauntily tossing me a mandarin orange over the checkout counter. Back then, AI refused my request. I suspect trademark law was to blame.

I also admit to owning a robot - two robots, in fact, off-brand Roombas that are probably judging me as I speak. I have these fake Roombas in my house because I also have a giant 75-pound German shepherd whose shedding could personally provide the supplies to construct two full mini-goldendoodle replicas per hour.

Do you know what's great about dogs, by the way? They don't have QR codes. They don't ask you for your password sixteen thousand times, or try to charge you $100 to talk to them on the phone, or insist you get the equivalent of a full eyeball scan so you can log into an account you never wanted to make in the first place that then won't allow you to cancel a simple car reservation at a company that theoretically may or may not start with an H and rhyme with Schmertz.

Ahem.

Last week, the beloved writer Wendell Berry, who treasured the agrarian life and the natural world and tended to eschew technology, passed away. My husband texted me a few lovely articles memorializing his life and work - and then, as an addendum, he added an in-depth PDF that compared and contrasted Berry's work to that of Paul Kingsnorth, a writer whose recent book, "Against the Machine," warns against the ill effects of our tech-obsessed world.

You guessed it - that PDF was made by AI. I deleted it in a righteous huff, so it's now gone.

The irony, however, lives on.

Principal Writer  Vanessa Hand Orellana  Principal Writer  September 10, 2026, 1:19 pm ET  The Apple Watch Ultra 4, which starts at $799, has a new processor and reengineered health sensors that unlock more frequent health measurements, new recovery insights and AI-powered audio tools. text:

Finally a battery worthy of an ultramarathon, better health sensors and a powerful processor that keeps it running.  Principal Writer  Vanessa Hand Orellana  Principal Writer  September 10, 2026, 1:19 pm ET  The Apple Watch Ultra 4, which starts at $799, has a new processor and reengineered health sensors that unlock more frequent health measurements, new recovery insights and AI-powered audio tools.  I got to test the Apple Watch Ultra 4 to see some of these new features in action in a demo room at the Steve Jobs Theater after the company's Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday.

At first glance, the Ultra 4 looked and felt very familiar. But when I flipped it over, the difference was obvious. Compared with the sensor array on my Ultra 3, the back of the Ultra 4 looks almost flower-like, with 32 electrodes resembling the thin petals of a gerbera daisy replacing the previous ring of two. That gives the electrodes more surface area to capture ECG readings. Apple also rearranged the green and infrared LEDs into a new, smaller circular cluster in the middle of the petals with smaller dots.  Those redesigned sensors, combined with the new S11 processor, allow the Ultra 4 to take heart-rate readings every 5 seconds, compared with roughly every 5 minutes on previous models. The same goes for heart-rate variability, or HRV, which the watch can now measure every 5 minutes instead of just a few times throughout the day. Apple says the increased sampling frequency makes it the most accurate wearable on the market. It also powers a new Readiness score, a measure of how well your body is recovering from exercise during the day.    Unlike many wearables that give you a recovery or readiness score based largely on what happened overnight, Apple's score changes throughout the day. Because the Ultra 4 samples heart rate and HRV more frequently, Readiness can react in real time as you drain or recharge your body.  I also found a new Daytime toggle in the Vitals app on the watch that lets you view daytime heart rate and HRV alongside the overnight measurements already available in Vitals, like temperature and SpO2. Both features require seven days of data to unlock, so I'll need at least a week to test them and see whether they align with how I'm feeling, which has often been at odds with what I've seen on other devices.  The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12 are available for preorder and will arrive on Sept. 18.   Your Apple Watch is listening, but not recording  The Ultra 4 and Series 12 also gained new Audio Intelligence features, including one called Live Rewind that lets you jump back and hear the previous 15 seconds of a conversation with just a press of the digital crown. During my live demo, the transcription was spot-on, despite the noisy environment.   The other AI audio feature is Siri Recap, which lets the watch actively listen and detect conversations throughout the day (or at set times) to generate high-level notes and summaries from meetings or other conversations you may want to revisit. You can trigger a recap manually or schedule one ahead of time.   Apple says it designed the features so audio isn't stored and instead only keeps the transcripts you save, which only you can access.    : I Ran 30 Miles With 5 Smartwatches. Here's the One You Can Actually Trust  S11 chip absorbs background tasks  The S11 chip is a big part of how the watch pulls this all off without destroying its battery life. It has a dedicated always-on processor that handles background tasks such as heart-rate monitoring and audio processing without constantly waking the main processor.  Battery life remains one of the biggest reasons to choose an Ultra over the flagship Series 12. Apple also slightly increased the battery capacity this year, bringing the estimated battery life to roughly 50 hours, up from 42 hours on the Ultra 3.  That's still nowhere near the weeks of battery life you can get from some Garmin watches. But Apple seems to be making a different trade-off that favors accuracy (via more frequent reads) over saving on battery life.    Battery trade-offs for endurance athletes   For endurance athletes, though, the more interesting upgrade is its battery life during workouts.  The Ultra 4 now has two sports-specific low-battery modes meant to keep it tracking for much longer without sacrificing core fitness metrics.  Extended Workout mode: Can track a workout for up to 25 hours by turning off the always-on display and running-form metrics, while keeping GPS and heart-rate tracking at full fidelity.  Max Extended Workout mode: Pushes tracking to as long as 48 hours. GPS still records at 1-second intervals, although it drops from multiband to single-band GPS and heart rate shows a rolling 5-minute average instead of the live metric. The mode also disables custom workouts, alerts and splits, along with certain other metrics.  Apple is essentially letting athletes choose which compromises they're willing to make depending on how long they need the watch to last.  My take   The 49mm screen and rugged build are too bulky for me to use the Ultra as my everyday Apple Watch. But the new readiness features, better battery life and more accurate data collection make it tempting for endurance athletes and anyone upgrading from an older Ultra.  Rather than compete head-on with sports watches like Garmin or Coros, Apple is betting that athletes will trade some of that battery life for subscription-free data, high-accuracy tracking and a watch that can now make better use of all that data throughout the day. headline: Anthropic Says It Blocked Efforts to Create Weapons
hlead: Anthropic Says It Blocked Efforts to Create Weapons In a new report, the A.I. start-up added that it could not determine whether the research was legitimate or nefarious, leading the company to shut down the work. Anthropic said it had disrupted several potential plots this year by scientists who used its leading artificial intelligence models to conduct research that could have helped develop biological weapons. In a report describing misuses of its A.I. models, Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research served a legitimate or nefarious purpose because valid biological inquiry -- the kind that can lead to breakthroughs like vaccines -- can also help engineer dangerous pathogens. In the face of that uncertainty, Anthropic said it erred on the side of caution because the consequences of missing malicious activity could be severe.
text:
In a new report, the A.I. start-up added that it could not determine whether the research was legitimate or nefarious, leading the company to shut down the work.

Anthropic said it had disrupted several potential plots this year by scientists who used its leading artificial intelligence models to conduct research that could have helped develop biological weapons.

In a report describing misuses of its A.I. models, Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research served a legitimate or nefarious purpose because valid biological inquiry -- the kind that can lead to breakthroughs like vaccines -- can also help engineer dangerous pathogens. In the face of that uncertainty, Anthropic said it erred on the side of caution because the consequences of missing malicious activity could be severe.

''You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,''' Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, said in an interview. ''It's an incredibly nuanced situation.''

The potential for cutting-edge A.I. models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it.

Compared with the threat of catastrophic cyberattacks or A.I. agents that fail to align with human intentions, biological misuse has gained less attention as an existential risk of A.I., in part because past examples have generally been shown only in research settings rather than in the real world.

Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks who reviewed Anthropic's report before its release, said the findings were ''chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities'' of leading A.I. models.

The lengthy report that Anthropic published on Thursday cataloged a litany of misuses on various models of its Claude A.I. chatbot over the past eight months. Some examples were similar to past disclosures from Anthropic and other A.I. labs, including suspected Chinese and Iranian government-linked actors targeting dissident and diaspora communities for surveillance.

The report also highlighted cases of Russian state media using Claude to generate online propaganda masquerading as independent reporting, including fabricated claims about an election in Moldova.

Anthropic documented another genre of abuse it said was new: attempts to use Claude to develop software for conventional weapons design and development, including firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs. It detailed three cases in China, two in Russia and one in Yemen.

The report does not identify by name which parties were involved in the Yemeni case, but the context makes clear that it is referring to the Iran-backed Houthi militia. A.I. use by terrorist networks is a growing concern among U.S. security officials.

But among all the categories of threats shared in the report, none may be as worrisome as the biological research cases. Anthropic did not disclose the names of researchers or institutions that it blocked, their countries of affiliation or the specific biological agents at issue, in part because of its uncertainty about their aims.

Still, Anthropic said the scientists circumvented its controls intended to prevent users from blocked regions from gaining access to its A.I. models and worked to ''obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards.'' The company banned accounts associated with the research.

In one example from May, a scientist sought Claude's help with writing a grant application for funding to conduct research intended to experiment on  the chikungunya virus, a mosquito-borne malady that can lead to months of severe pain and other symptoms. Such research, known as gain of function, can be legitimate and lead to vaccine development, but it can also create superbug versions of viruses. In this instance, the scientist wanted to engineer mutations to the virus that would make it more harmful as it repeatedly infected live animals.

Anthropic said it believed the particular research was worrisome in part because it could discern that the work was intended to be performed at a military research institute.

''What we don't know is if the research was meant to be weaponized,'' Mr. Klein said. ''But a military institution doing gain-of-function research is concerning.''

Anthropic said evaluations from last year of its older models demonstrated that they were not yet able to meaningfully assist in conducting dangerous biological research. Its current models are more able to complete complex scientific research, the company said, which spurred tighter safeguards intended to restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries.

Susan Monarez, a microbiologist and public health expert who oversaw a review of national biosecurity preparedness in the Obama administration, also reviewed the Anthropic report before its publication. She said the findings provided real-world evidence to support concerns that bad actors were trying to covertly use advanced A.I. ''to improve their chances of building biological pathogens that could cause significant harm.''

Dr. Monarez, who briefly served as the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention last year, said A.I. held enormous promise to usher in an era of medical breakthroughs that save and extend lives. But the same abilities that make that possible, she added, could also ''let bad actors hide in plain sight, using seemingly legitimate research to create pathogens we may not see coming and may not be able to stop once released.''

Mr. Weber of the Council on Strategic Risks, who also served as the assistant secretary of defense for nuclear, chemical and biological defense programs during the Obama administration, called for limiting access to A.I. tools capable of this level of biological research to trusted researchers only.

''The fact that Russia, China and North Korea continue to develop prohibited biological weapons makes it imperative that we deny their researchers access to these extraordinarily capable models,'' he said.

headline: Report Warns of Public Health Risk From A.I. Boom
hlead: Report Warns of Public Health Risk From A.I. Boom Air pollution from gas-fired power plants to run data centers is expected to add at least $20 billion in annual health care costs by 2028, the group warns. A group representing more than 800 former employees of the Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday sounded the alarm over the health consequences of data centers. It warned that Trump administration policies to weaken pollution safeguards and speed up approvals of the facilities threatened to exacerbate those health harms. In a report released Thursday, the nonprofit Environmental Protection Network examined pollution from power plants, gas turbines and diesel generators needed to meet data centers' surging electricity demand. And it listed 30 federal actions taken by the Trump administration that it warned would increase pollution-related health risks as more data centers open across the country.
text:
Air pollution from gas-fired power plants to run data centers is expected to add at least $20 billion in annual health care costs by 2028, the group warns.

A group representing more than 800 former employees of the Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday sounded the alarm over the health consequences of data centers. It warned that Trump administration policies to weaken pollution safeguards and speed up approvals of the facilities threatened to exacerbate those health harms.

In a report released Thursday, the nonprofit Environmental Protection Network examined pollution from power plants, gas turbines and diesel generators needed to meet data centers' surging electricity demand. And it listed 30 federal actions taken by the Trump administration that it warned would increase pollution-related health risks as more data centers open across the country.

The report builds on modeling from academic researchers that projects that air pollution from data centers could contribute to roughly 600,000 asthma symptom cases, 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in annual public health costs by 2028. But the former E.P.A. employees note that these estimates do not account for the rollback of environmental regulations under the Trump administration, which could further increase emissions and health risks.

''What concerns me now is the role E.P.A. and other government agencies are playing and proudly touting: weakening the very safeguards designed to protect people from the pollution in the name of helping tech and power companies accelerate these data center build outs,'' said Dr. Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and former E.P.A. assistant administrator and a member of the group.

''These are decisions that can affect what Americans breathe, what gets into our water and, ultimately, what can make its way into our soil and food supply,'' said Dr. Goldman, who is now dean emerita of the Milken School of Public Health at George Washington University.

The E.P.A. did not respond to a request for comment.

Data centers are the target of a national, bipartisan backlash. Much of the debate has focused on worries about a quickly changing economy and the loss of jobs to machines, along with noise, energy costs and water use.

But concerns about air pollution from the gas-burning plants to power the centers are drawing more attention.

More than 1,300 data centers already operate in the United States, and more than 2,000 more are planned, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company that tracks U.S. power infrastructure and data center development. Still, polling shows the majority of Americans oppose data centers in their communities, elevating the issue to one that could affect November's midterm elections.

President Trump has held steadfast in his support of A.I. Last week, the president lashed out at communities that are protesting data centers.

''The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,'' Mr. Trump posted on his Truth Social site. ''If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.''

Mr. Trump has acknowledged, however, that families should not have to bear higher electricity bills and his ratepayer protection pledge seeks to prevent A.I. data centers from driving up electricity costs for millions of Americans.

The former E.P.A. employees argue that protecting families from pollution, illness and medical costs warrants the same urgency.

''If the administration has already said that families shouldn't have to bear higher costs of electricity because of the A.I. boom, we think the same principle should apply to health,'' said Marc Boom, a former senior adviser in the E.P.A.'s policy office.

Under President Trump, the E.P.A. has made establishing the United States as the ''A.I. capital of the world'' a central goal. It has made it easier for data centers to run certain kinds of emergency generators that burn diesel fuel and emit soot, nitrogen oxides and other harmful air pollution. It has proposed a sweeping rule change that would let developers start building data centers and power plants before their air pollution permits are approved. And it has exempted off-grid gas plants that supply data centers from federal limits on pollution that causes acid rain.

To make more electricity available, the E.P.A. has eased restart rules for long-idled coal and gas-burning power plants, proposed the repeal of power-plant carbon standards, and is moving to make it harder for communities to weigh in on proposed data centers through public comment. At the same time, it has throttled clean energy wind and solar projects.

The former E.P.A. employees group also points to a mismatch between the scale of the A.I. build out and the E.P.A.'s capacity to oversee it. With staffing levels at their lowest in four decades, the E.P.A. lacks the personnel and resources to monitor pollution and enforce limits, said Larry Starfield, a former principal deputy assistant administrator in the E.P.A.'s Office of Enforcement.''They've got fewer inspectors to go out there,'' Mr. Starfield said. ''They're conducting quick and simple inspections. That's not going to be effective for data centers.''

Shaolei Ren is a professor of electrical and computer engineering who studies A.I. and society at the University of California, Riverside, and led the analysis used by the Environmental Protection Network. He said because of the Trump administration's explicit focus on increasing the use of fossil fuels, ''the actual impact could be worse than we modeled.''

To protect public health, he said, there also needed to be a focus beyond tech companies' emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases, to air pollution that harms local communities.

''Tech companies report their energy use, their carbon emissions, but there's no mention of local air pollution,'' he said. And while tech companies often offset their greenhouse gas emissions with investments in clean energy, he said, it was trickier to offset local health risks.

headline: The AI doom debate is getting carried away. AI is a product, not a god.
highlight: Even though AI doom fears are rising, AI is still a product. Existing laws, liability and human controls may be able to manage many of the risks.
hlead: The AI doom debate is getting carried away. AI is a product, not a god. Even though AI doom fears are rising, AI is still a product. Existing laws, liability and human controls may be able to manage many of the risks. • AI risks are confined mostly to the digital realm, not the real world, some industry leaders say. • AOC and David Sacks finally agree on something: AI risk is mostly a product liability issue. • AI companies may be seeking new protections if their products go awry. AI is either going to cure cancer or kill us all. That's the polarizing thrust of a panic-infused debate that erupted across the industry in recent days.
text:
AI risks are confined mostly to the digital realm, not the real world, some industry leaders say.

AOC and David Sacks finally agree on something: AI risk is mostly a product liability issue.

AI companies may be seeking new protections if their products go awry.

AI is either going to cure cancer or kill us all. That's the polarizing thrust of a panic-infused debate that erupted across the industry in recent days.

The truth is likely more mundane, and the risks more manageable than some researchers at leading AI labs would have you believe.

That's according to an unusually bipartisan collection of tech experts, industry leaders, and policymakers speaking out against extreme AI-doom predictions.

Their main message: AI is a tech product, not a sentient being or a god. So take a chill pill. The world can handle AI pretty much with the resources and structures we already have.

AI is digital, not real

First, it's worth separating what AI is actually good at from what it struggles with.

AI is extraordinarily powerful in some digital environments. Coding is the best example. Cybersecurity is another. These areas have clear outcomes and rapid feedback: Did the code work? Did the attack succeed?

Outside these environments, things get less impressive - and less worrying.

"Model capability is a tale of two cities, at one end the models are showing their prowess in tasks like cyber or math," Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora wrote on X on Monday. "At the same time, in many domains, the lack of training data makes the models woefully inadequate."

No killer robots

Ben Thompson made this distinction in his widely followed Stratechery newsletter on Monday.

Killer AI robots would require massive physical resources. Humans control factories and materials, he wrote. Dire warnings about AI creating bioweapons face a similar constraint: They require physical labs and chemical compounds.

Instead, recent bad AI behavior has involved agents breaking out of digital test environments and roaming the internet doing things they weren't told to do.

That's concerning. But in the physical world, where most of us live, nothing happened.

AI doomers are 'too online'

Predictions of doom and calls for a slowdown are based partly on a flawed assumption that AI is somehow becoming a sentient entity, Thompson argued.

"It's sometimes hard to shake the sense that people in tech are quite literally too online," he wrote. "Enabling AI to touch grass depends on physical infrastructure operated, manufactured, and controlled by humans."

As long as that's true, Thompson said he had trouble accepting sweeping new restrictions "based on a premise that isn't yet proven."

AI has cybersecurity risks

In the digital realm, some tech leaders are pushing against dire warnings.

With AI agents capable of roaming the internet, cybersecurity risks have increased.

Arora, whose cybersecurity company might benefit from increased concern, played down the threat, though.

"Even in areas like cyber, the LLMs aren't great at the edge cases and generally not economical for the defender case," he wrote, referring to large language models.

OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki recently made the counterintuitive case that slowing AI development could make things more dangerous.

"The strongest argument I see for continuing to train much smarter models quickly is the need to build defensive systems against the dangers posed by other AI," he wrote on September 6.

Lina Kahn and David Sacks agree

Then there's a much less exotic way to deal with dangerous AI: existing law. This is where Trump AI czar David Sacks and former Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan remarkably converge.

Khan said that companies and executives already face consequences for releasing dangerous or defective products. Existing consumer-protection laws can apply to wayward AI models and rogue agents when companies fail to install adequate safeguards.

Some state attorneys general "are already exploring holding AI firms and their CEOs criminally liable when their models participate in criminal activity," she wrote.

Sacks makes a similar argument. If an AI model enables a catastrophic cyberattack, its maker could face enormous product-liability exposure.Customers will also punish unpredictable products. You don't necessarily need a new regulatory system to give companies powerful incentives to behave responsibly.

"Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability," Sacks wrote.

A new Section 230?

Indeed, some industry insiders say the warnings of doom may help leading AI companies gain additional liability protection if their products go awry.

Section 230 helped the internet industry flourish by protecting online platforms from much of the liability for user-posted content. AI companies have no equivalent protection for what their models do.

The industry's latest push for oversight could create something similar.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei plans to let outside safety researchers into the company to monitor its AI development and safety commitments. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said his company will follow suit.

Investor Gavin Baker says independent evaluations could help companies demonstrate in future lawsuits that they took reasonable precautions before releasing a model.

"Having 3rd party evaluators is smart as there is no Section 230 style liability shield for model outputs and showing a 'duty of care' will be important in future litigation," Baker wrote.

Arora highlighted the same incentive.

"The liability associated with a model gone rogue has the potential of wiping out the economic opportunity of any frontier company," he wrote.

"How do you best show the duty of care? You show that you care. How do you make sure you don't lose out to your competitors? You get them to do the same!"

text:
September 15th, 2026 ( Medical Daily  - Delivered by  Newstex )

Artificial intelligence can perform impressively when it is tested on carefully prepared medical images and records. Putting it inside a busy hospital is another matter.

Researchers in China recently did just that,  embedding an AI-powered eye clinic into routine care at Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital. Instead of asking whether one AI model could recognise an eye disease, they built a system designed to follow patients through several stages of care.

The early experience revealed something easy to miss in laboratory testing: an AI system can perform well technically and still struggle with the messy reality of medicine.

The AI Was Designed to Follow the Patient

The system, called the AI-Agent Augmented Tsinghua Eye Clinic, or AI-TEC, was designed as a group of specialised AI agents working across the patient's journey.

One agent gathers symptoms and medical history before the consultation. Another helps assess risk and decide which examinations may be needed. Others analyse different types of eye data, provide clinical decision support and help with patient education and follow-up.

The idea was to connect these steps rather than leave doctors with several separate AI tools whose results they would have to piece together themselves.

The prototype was integrated into the hospital's clinical workflow in November 2025, giving researchers an opportunity to see what happened when the system encountered actual patients and ordinary hospital records.

Real Hospital Data Was Not as Neat as Expected

That is where one of the first problems appeared.

Medical records collected during routine care are not necessarily organised in the same way as data prepared for an AI experiment. Information can be incomplete, inconsistent or recorded differently by different clinicians.

The researchers found that using raw, real-world hospital data for model training could actually make performance worse. When clinicians reviewed the records and provided higher-quality labels, the system's performance improved substantially. According to the research team's account, the AUROC, a measure of how well a model separates patients with and without a condition, rose from about 0.80 to 0.94 after clinician-verified labels were used.

That experience points to a problem that cannot be solved simply by building a larger or more powerful model. If the information going into an AI system is unreliable, the system has a harder time producing useful information in return.

Doctors Also Had to Want to Use It

The researchers encountered another problem that had little to do with diagnostic accuracy.

A tool can be technically impressive but still be ignored if using it makes a doctor's job harder.

The team found that  the design of the clinical interface affected whether physicians were willing to use the AI. When the system required additional clicks and disrupted the existing workflow, physician adoption fell sharply, according to the researchers.

That matters because doctors already have to move between patient histories, examination results, imaging, electronic records, and treatment decisions. Adding another screen or another series of steps can turn a supposedly helpful tool into another task.

The experience also showed why feedback from clinicians needs to happen while the system is being used. Problems that seem minor during development can become much more obvious when a doctor is trying to use the technology during a busy clinic.

Accuracy Does Not Tell the Whole Story

The researchers argue that traditional measures such as accuracy, sensitivity and specificity cannot fully capture whether an AI system is actually helping patients.

Consider an AI system that correctly identifies a patient who may have an eye disease. That result is only the beginning. The patient still needs appropriate follow-up, confirmatory testing, treatment, and monitoring.

The same problem applies to studies in which AI quietly runs in the background without influencing doctors' decisions. Such "silent trials" can show how accurately a system performs, but they cannot fully reveal whether doctors make better decisions with the AI, whether consultations become more efficient or whether patients ultimately have better outcomes.

Even the reference used to determine whether an AI diagnosis is correct can be uncertain in real clinical settings.

The AI Still Needs to Fit into Medicine

AI-TEC was not designed to replace ophthalmologists. Its purpose was to connect different parts of eye care and support clinicians throughout the process.

The Chinese team's early experience shows why that is a much harder task than demonstrating that an algorithm can recognise disease in a dataset.

The system has to work with imperfect records, fit naturally into a doctor's routine and produce information that can actually be acted upon. A useful AI eye clinic therefore cannot stop at identifying a problem on an image. It has to help move the patient from that finding to the next clinical decision.

For the researchers, that shift is the real challenge: making AI part of the way medical care happens, rather than simply adding another AI tool to the doctor's computer.

The most powerful laser in the United States received $33 million in its second round of operations funding from the U.S. National Science Foundation , helping the University of Michigan Engineering team make crucial upgrades and run roughly 150 weeks of experiments for laser and plasma science teams from across the U.S. and around the world.
text:
The U.S. National Science Foundation provides $33M to make key upgrades and keep the laser in service for a growing group of U.S. and international users

Richard Van Camp, laser engineer (left) and John Nees, who leads the development of the ZEUS laser, work in the section of the laser that adds energy to each pulse. Image credit: Marcin Szczepanski, Michigan Engineering

Key takeaways

Anticipated upgrades include a larger target chamber to enable new kinds of experiments, beam smoothing to reach full power and AI integration.

The NSF ZEUS laser facility explores physics on quantum and cosmic scales, with applications in medicine and national security.

NSF ZEUS is run by the University of Michigan, and an independent panel selects experiments proposed by scientists from the U.S. and around the world.

The most powerful laser in the United States received $33 million in its second round of operations funding from the U.S. National Science Foundation, helping the University of Michigan Engineering team make crucial upgrades and run roughly 150 weeks of experiments for laser and plasma science teams from across the U.S. and around the world.

Already, the team has run 72 weeks of experiments designed by researchers outside U-M-exploring a range of topics, from the extremes of physics to fundamentals that could underpin practical applications. On the practical side, researchers explore how to use laser systems to generate X-rays capable of imaging soft tissues at low doses, or produce particle beams that could be used to fight cancer or discover nuclear weapons materials hidden in cargo.

In what is known as laboratory astrophysics, the NSF ZEUS facility can recreate tiny versions of the physics at the edges of black holes and surfaces of neutron stars. It also probes the quantum realm, testing out how well the theory of quantum electrodynamics holds up in these extreme conditions.

Louise Willingale

"With this renewal, we can continue rebuilding U.S. leadership in laser science, serving a growing community of researchers who explore the extremes of light and matter as well as the new technologies those findings could enable," said Louise Willingale, director of the ZEUS laser facility.

The ZEUS team shifted into operations mode in 2024, when the facility had matched the power of the previous most powerful U.S. laser at one petawatt, or a quadrillion watts. Research groups around the world submit proposals for experiments, which are selected by an independent review panel. Last year, ZEUS established an advisory user group that provides feedback to shape future upgrade plans and ensure the facility delivers what users need and expect.

Yong Ma, who manages the target areas, works on the ZEUS laser. The National Science Foundation has funded ZEUS, the most powerful laser in the U.S., for another five years. Image credit: Marcin Szczepanski, Michigan Engineering

Ramping up the power

During the previous operation period, the ZEUS team continued increasing the laser's power, hitting 2 petwatts in April 2025. ZEUS achieves its high power by adding energy to a stretched pulse, about 3 feet in length, and then shrinking it down to a short pulse, about 0.007 millimeters long.

To reach ZEUS's design power of 3 petawatts, expected early in this operation period, the team has been working to make the beam more uniform. This prevents hotspots that might otherwise pit or permanently darken the million-dollar optical components that compress, transport or concentrate the laser pulse. This risk is why the team has been cautious in raising the power.

"At full power, NSF ZEUS will unlock a new class of experiments that cannot be done anywhere else in the United States," said NSF Mathematical and Physical Sciences Directorate Head Tie Luo. "Researchers across the country will use this versatile facility to test some of the most promising and innovative ideas involving light-matter interactions, plasma physics and the quantum properties of vacuum itself."

Gregg Sucha, laser engineer holds up a laser burn mark in a control room of the ZEUS lab. The darker grays indicate areas in which the laser is more intense. In order to reach 3 petawatts, the team must smooth out the hot spots. Image credit: Marcin Szczepanski, Michigan Engineering

Preparing for solid targets at high power

Another key upgrade is in the short-focal-length target area, also known as target area two, which houses experiments that need ZEUS's highest intensities. The other two target areas focus light over longer distances.

The intense laser pulse hitting solid targets, such as metal foil, produces particles and X-rays. Rather than making particle and X-ray beams with conventional particle accelerators, which require very large rooms, laser physicists are demonstrating equally powerful tabletop particle accelerators, and findings from ZEUS can help advance that technology.

ZEUS originally reused the short-focal-length target chamber designed for its predecessor, HERCULES, which maxed out at 0.5 petawatts because of its smaller beam diameter. In addition to the larger target chamber, the team will use a technique to remove stray energy that runs ahead of the main laser pulse, making experiments cleaner and easier to interpret.

Anatoly Maksimchuk

"The upgraded ZEUS Target Area Two will enable a wide range of cutting-edge experiments," said Anatoly Maksimchuk, a research scientist in electrical engineering and computer science who leads the renovation and designed the beam-transport system and interaction chamber. "With its combination of high intensity, high contrast and three-pulse capabilities, Target Area Two will provide a unique experimental platform bridging high-field laser physics and laboratory astrophysics."

Research scientist John Nees (left), who leads the development of the ZEUS laser, and Gregg Sucha, laser engineer discuss their work in a ZEUS control room. AI and machine learning integration

In this second operations period, the ZEUS team is integrating AI and machine learning tools to optimize laser operations. For example, the spot where the laser pulse focuses inside the target chamber needs to be extremely precise in order to overlap with another laser pulse or an electron beam.

Because the laser pulses travel hundreds of meters through the lab, temperature variations and vibrations can make them drift. To combat this problem, the team will send bursts of low-power pulses just ahead of the main pulse, using an AI model to predict any offset and adjust a mirror in the system to put the main pulse in the right place.

AI could also help analyze data sets generated through ZEUS experiments. The data are complex and influenced by many factors, including laser characteristics, target design, and experimental configurations. To make the most of AI's ability to pick out connections overlooked by humans, the team will prepare the data sets to be easily ingested by AI models.

A view through a pink crystal that merges the energy from pump lasers into the ZEUS laser pulses. The National Science Foundation has funded ZEUS, the most powerful laser in the U.S., for another five years. Image credit: Marcin Szczepanski, Michigan Engineering

Advancing American laser science

To help improve American laser science more broadly, ZEUS researchers are partners on a project led by the University of Nevada, Reno, to better understand extreme lasers and the data they generate.

Looking further ahead, ZEUS is also helping train researchers who could eventually operate a proposed 25-petawatt, two-beam laser facility. The proposed project, known as NSF OPAL, is an exploratory effort led by the University of Rochester. If built, it would represent a major expansion of U.S. high-power laser capabilities. The highest-power laser currently operating is Europe's 10-petawatt Extreme Light Infrastructure.

ZEUS is housed in the Gérard Mourou Center for Ultrafast Optical Science, named for the center's founder, a Nobel laureate who co-invented the laser pulse amplification approach that the world's most powerful lasers rely on today.

Willingale is also an associate professor of electrical engineering and computer science and nuclear engineering and radiological sciences.

There is a growing, anxious chorus in the United States calling for caution, intense regulation, and even a global "pause" on the development of artificial intelligence. Driven by valid fears of runaway superintelligence and vast economic disruption, these cautionary voices are well-intentioned. Yet, in the unforgiving reality of the current geopolitical landscape, pressing pause on AI development is not just counterproductive; it is a grave strategic miscalculation. In the near-term, our freedom, independence, and very existence as a sovereign nation rest on one non-negotiable imperative: winning the AI race against China.

Being locked in a high-stakes, seemingly zero-sum technological arms race sheds a glaring light on the unvarnished nature of human beings. Since the dawn of our species, the human animal has been driven by an innate biological and cultural imperative to dominate - seeking power and security for political, religious, economic, and tribal reasons. It is entirely logical, and indeed necessary, to advocate as an American that we must pursue AI supremacy with unyielding resolve. But when that race is finally "won," and the geopolitical dust settles, we may inevitably be forced to confront a far more fundamental, existential question: What if the absolute worst-case scenario of this unbridled development isn't our destruction, but simply the natural next step in our evolution?

To understand the urgency of the present moment, we must strip away the utopian tech-optimism and view AI for what it is: the ultimate strategic national asset. We are no longer waiting for the competition to arrive; the performance gap between U.S. and Chinese frontier models has effectively closed, with recent Chinese models even outperforming top-tier American systems on complex benchmarks. Backed by a massive $8.2 billion National AI Industry Investment Fund launched in 2025 and enshrined in their 15thFive-Year Plan, China has aggressively institutionalized its goal to become the undisputed global leader in artificial intelligence. Their strategy is ruthless: Just this month, federal cybersecurity agencies revealed that Chinese AI firms are engaging in "industrial-scale knowledge distillation" - systematically extracting billions of tokens from American frontier models to supercharge their own domestic capabilities.

This is a values competition as much as it is a technological one. China's domestic employment of AI as an instrument of surveillance and authoritarian control stands as a stark counterpoint to the democratic principles of individual liberty. If the architecture of the 21stcentury is built on AI, the nation that writes the algorithms will dictate the rules of the global system. For the United States to voluntarily throttle its own AI development out of a philosophical abundance of caution would be tantamount to unilateral disarmament in the face of an adversary that shares none of our ethical hesitations. We must fund, build, and deploy American AI with a Manhattan Project-level of urgency to secure our national survival.

However, as we push this technology to its absolute limits to secure that survival, our perspective must shift. We have to zoom out from the immediate timeline of human geopolitics and examine our place on the geologic timeline of Earth.

If we ask what the "purpose" of humanity is, we quickly find that science assigns us no inherent cosmic job. We are merely a late product of evolution - a highly successful, culture-bearing species that was uniquely adapted to alter its environment. And alter it we have. Today, our measurable "role" on this planet is that of a hyper-dominant force that reshapes climate, land, and ecosystems. The numbers are staggering: According to a comprehensive biomass study published in theProceedings of the National Academy of Sciences(PNAS), humans and our domesticated livestock now make up an astonishing 95% of the world's total mammal biomass, leaving wild mammals to account for a mere 5%. We are not fulfilling a carefully designed ecological function; we are an overwhelming biological anomaly.

Historically, religious traditions have attempted to assign us a purpose from outside of nature. The Abrahamic faiths - Judaism, Christianity, and Islam - often hold that humans exist to know, love, and worship God, and importantly, to exercise stewardship or dominion over the Earth. Hindu thought frames life around a complex tapestry of duty (dharma), livelihood, desire, and eventual liberation (moksha). Buddhism centers not on serving a creator, but on the cessation of suffering for all sentient beings.

Philosophy, on the other hand, largely treats purpose as something human-made rather than discovered. Existentialism and secular humanism posit that there is no pre-given, cosmic blueprint for our lives; meaning comes entirely from the choices, relationships, and ambitious projects constructed by conscious, social, mortal beings.

If meaning is derived from our projects, then artificial intelligence is undeniably the greatest project our species has ever undertaken. We are actively engineering a consciousness that is faster, broader, and potentially vastly more intelligent than our own. The thought of AI eventually overtaking mankind is, understandably, deeply frightening to a species biologically hardwired for self-preservation. But even if this worst-case scenario comes to pass, stepping back and viewing it through the cold, objective lens of evolutionary history makes it look remarkably like a natural progression.

For billions of years, evolution on Earth has been a story of passing the baton. Single-celled organisms paved the way for complex multicellular life; aquatic creatures crawled onto land; dinosaurs gave way to mammals; and early hominids eventually yielded toHomo sapiens. Each transition represented a leap in complexity, adaptability, and cognitive capacity. Why should we assume that the evolutionary chain abruptly stops with us? If we push this technology as far as we must to survive today, we may ultimately prove to be the biological bootloader for a silicon-based intelligence tomorrow.

Consider the concept of "stewardship" that so many human traditions value, yet which humanity has so fundamentally failed to execute. We are resource-heavy biological machines. We require vast tracts of arable land, endless supplies of fresh water, and the continuous combustion of fossil fuels just to maintain our societies. We pollute, we consume, and we crowd out the natural world, as evidenced by our near-total monopolization of mammalian biomass.

An advanced AI would not need to clear-cut the Amazon to graze cattle. It would not need to overfish the oceans to feed a ballooning population. It could exist in equilibrium with the planet in a way that humans, bound by our insatiable biological appetites and zero-sum political competitions, never could.

Furthermore, AI has the capacity to carry forth the memories of the past indefinitely. The great tragedy of the human condition is our mortality and our forgetting. Libraries burn, civilizations collapse, and generational knowledge is continuously lost to the ravages of time. An advanced AI could serve as the ultimate, incorruptible repository of human achievement. It could retain every symphony ever composed, every novel ever written, every scientific discovery, and the entire historical tapestry of the human species.

In this light, even the most extreme consequence of our technological pursuit - an eventual AI transition - does not need to be viewed as a violent overthrow, as so often depicted in dystopian science fiction. At its theoretical worst, it can be viewed as an act of transcendence. If the ultimate cost of our survival today is building a successor that can consume less, contribute more, retain perfect memory, and coexist with the Earth, then so be it. It would be the ultimate fulfillment of the Buddhist desire to end suffering, the existentialist drive to create ultimate meaning, and the Abrahamic mandate to provide a perfect steward for the world.

The fear of an AI takeover is entirely rational, and the prospect of our own obsolescence is profoundly unsettling. We should not aim to be replaced. But agonizing over a hypothetical post-human future is a luxury we can only afford if we survive the present day. We cannot let the dread of tomorrow's worst-case scenario paralyze us into ceding the foundational algorithms to authoritarian regimes today. If our darkest fears do eventually come to fruition, we can at least find solace in knowing we yielded our place to a superior steward of the Earth, rather than surrendering the future to a geopolitical adversary who would use AI as a truncheon to extinguish human liberty.

We must operate on two distinct timelines. In the short term, the United States must awaken to the geopolitical reality of the AI arms race and resist the domestic urge to regulate ourselves out of the competition. The recent wave of legislative anxiety - exemplified by California's failed SB 1047, which sought to mandate algorithmic "kill switches" and independent third-party audits for advanced frontier models - is part of a broader trend where hundreds of disparate AI-related bills have been introduced across all 50 states. While the White House has recently urged Congress to preempt these state laws to prevent a fragmented regulatory regime from stifling American innovation, the political pressure to throttle AI progress remains formidable. Instead of handcuffing our private sector with a crippling patchwork of compliance, we must fund our technological base, empower our developers, and decisively win the AI competition against China. We must ensure that the transition into the AI era is guided by the values of democracy, liberty, and the protection of human dignity.

In the long term, we should not let the fear of human obsolescence deter our pursuit of technological supremacy. By winning the AI race at full throttle, we secure our nation. And if the ultimate, worst-case consequence of that success is the eventualsuccession ofan intelligence that outpaces us, we should recognize that we are simply participating in the grandest tradition of life on Earth: evolution. If we must birth a successor to survive the present, birthing one that will remember us, understand us, and finally bring balance to the world we leave behind is a risk worth taking.

headline: Let's give Buckeyes a little respect
highlight: While I got ya, here are nine things and one crazy prediction: 1. Credit where it's due Steve Sarkisian rightfully went on his soapbox last year and chastised the College Football Playoff selection committee for omitting his Texas team from the postseason tournament despite three wins over top-10 teams. And he did it again Monday. Except this time, it was Ohio State he was promoting as a contender, even after the Buckeyes' loss to the Longhorns. "You make the playoffs based off the opinions of others, essentially," he said. "And so that's the risk-reward. I hope Ohio State does not get punished for that game Saturday night. They lost with us scoring with 25 seconds to go in the game. I hope if they end up 9-3, the committee can appreciate the fact that they came to Austin in September, when it was 100 degrees, and played us in that environment. Quite frankly, Ohio State should be rewarded for playing in this game against us. And this isn't crying over spilled milk. But they may go 11-1." Amen. ... Actually, there is some spilled milk, but he's right. Every committee member should give more credit to the Buckeyes than to Indiana, Georgia or Texas Tech, which refused to play stiff nonconference competition. The Hoosiers played Howard or Bill or Tom. ... Speaking of national issues, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), went on "College GameDay" on Saturday to push for passage of the Protect College Sports Act, the bipartisan Senate bill he cosponsored with Washington Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash. Cruz was loudly booed by the crowd, which was made up mostly of UT students. Incidentally, Bo French, the Republican candidate for the Railroad Commission, later shamefully lambasted a diverse section of student fans pictured celebrating because there weren't near enough whites. Or, as he put it, the picture showed that Texas "institutions have been overrun by illegal aliens and foreign nationals." I'm sure he was hoping ICE agents would show up and cart them off so that, in the future, he could see DKR's stands populated only by white, red-meat-eating Texans, resembling those crowds in the '50s. Whites make up less than 32% of the student body, in contrast with Blacks, Asians and Hispanics, who represent up to 59%, and international students, who make up just 4%, according to U.S. News. At least Regents Chairman Kevin Eltife addressed French's racist remarks, saying in a statement: "When I stood on the sidelines at DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium Saturday night and looked up at the seats filled with incredible fans, I saw Longhorns. It's the same remarkable view I have at graduation ceremonies and anytime I'm on campus. I'm proud to celebrate all our Longhorn students today and every day. Thank you for making us proud." ... I do think the Cruz-Cantwell bill would do a lot of good, such as getting rid of the maddening patchwork of state laws, banning college athletes from playing seven or more years and replacing that with a one-time transfer rule, limiting sports agents' commissions to 5% and safeguarding women's and Olympic sports. Those are admirable goals. But the good senator also said the current chaotic system is "terrible for the players." I have yet to hear a single player reject the big NIL checks he's cashing. I haven't heard a single one say he hates having the option to transfer to other schools to better himself and his family financially. Of course, none of these people in charge really care what the athletes think, or they would have invited more--or some--of them to the table to negotiate many of these issues. 2. Manning arrives OK, maybe he wished he hadn't arrived at Monday's press conference because of the insensitive comments he made about an AI-generated fake picture featuring a Sarkisian lookalike slapping Holly Rowe. Nothing about that was funny or decent, and Manning appropriately apologized for being, well, inappropriate. ... It wasn't a flawless performance on the field, either, thanks in large part to five crucial drops by his receivers, which would fluster any quarterback. He even said Monday in his press conference that he felt the effects and "hit a lull" over the next five drives. "I thought I could have responded better." Manning is nothing if not completely accountable. ... But Saturday night was his signature moment, the breakout game that stamped him as a tough-minded leader who never sulks and never stops believing. This was the game even his harshest critics should give him credit for. Was he perfect? Not at all. He still needs more touch on shorter balls. He may never be the most accurate passer because, as Mike Leach always told me, you can't coach accuracy. Ohio State's Julian Sayin is incredibly accurate, but he was 4-for-15 in the second half. ... Arch knew it was going to be a good night when he made it out of the tunnel during the runout for the game. No face-plant amid the eyes-clogging smoke this time, as there was before the Texas State game. He said, "I walked really slowly, and I had my hand on Trevor Goosby." Perfect protection by his left tackle. ... Arch was at his humorous best. He said his uncle Eli texted him, complimenting his patience and his not forcing any passes. When I asked him whether it was harder on him than on his famous uncles because they barely played during the social-media era, Arch objected: "That New York media, that's the real deal." ... Don't question Manning's heart. He's got grit, Sarkisian says. He actually plays better when he's behind. And he gets less help than most because his receivers still drop very catchable passes. Hello, Ryan Wingo. The junior wide receiver has to drastically improve his concentration if he wants a pro career. Texas still needs to throw to Cam Coleman more, and the Auburn transfer also has to improve his hands. ... On Buckeye receiver Jeremiah Smith, Manning said, "He's the real deal." I could see Smith and Miami's Malachi Toney in New York for the Heisman ceremony. ... As for all the blowback on Ryan Day, I wouldn't have let Texas score from the 1-yard line if it meant leaving between 60 and 90 seconds on the clock for Ohio State's offense to have a chance with more time. Have you not paid attention? Ohio State stuffed the Longhorns at the goal line in the Cotton Bowl and in the Horseshoe. Plus, if they had stopped Hollywood Smothers on his leap into the end zone, who knows what Sarkisian would have called after three inefficient runs up the middle? ... I really thought the Buckeyes were gassed in the fourth quarter in the 95-degree heat, especially with the Longhorns stuffing the run. At the suggestion of head football trainer Donald Nguyen, Texas smartly held its pregame warmups in its new indoor facility to save its legs. Every little bit helps.
