As for all the blowback on Ryan Day, I wouldn't have let Texas score from the 1-yard line if it meant leaving between 60 and 90 seconds on the clock for Ohio State's offense to have a chance with more time. Have you not paid attention? Ohio State stuffed the Longhorns at the goal line in the Cotton Bowl and in the Horseshoe. Plus, if they had stopped Hollywood Smothers on his leap into the end zone, who knows what Sarkisian would have called after three inefficient runs up the middle? ... I really thought the Buckeyes were gassed in the fourth quarter in the 95-degree heat, especially with the Longhorns stuffing the run. At the suggestion of head football trainer Donald Nguyen, Texas smartly held its pregame warmups in its new indoor facility to save its legs. Every little bit helps.

3. Ranking the rally

The top two for me, in order, will always be the 12-point rally to beat USC in the 2006 Rose Bowl and the comeback from a 14-0 hole at the end of three quarters against Arkansas to crush the Razorbacks' spirit forever in the Big Shootout in 1969. I really believe the improbable comeback to stun Ohio State ranks third because the Buckeyes looked dominant for three quarters, were ranked No. 1 and because the Longhorns earned -- weren't gifted by cheap turnovers, weren't lucky -- but earned the win by asserting their will with three consecutive scoring drives. Texas took that game. ... Sayin is an obvious first-round NFL quarterback, and Smith is better than Toney because he's bigger and more physical than the Miami receiver.

4. All things Horns

Besides the reliable Emmett Mosley V, who needs more targets for his sure hands and tight routes, three other Longhorns got tremendous love for their games. Sarkisian singled out defensive tackle Ian Geffrard, tight end Emaree Winston and left guard Dylan Sikorski. "I always knew Emaree was a gamer," Manning said. "He's a stud. He has some of the best hands on the team. I think he'll continue to do that going on this season." Winston will be called upon a lot, moreso with the knee injury to Nick Townsend. He's got big 10-inch hands. ... Sarkisian said he had planned to rotate Sikorski and Laurence Seymore III, but Sikorski was playing so well, "we just kind of let it go." This was the best performance by Texas' offensive line since the 2023 win in Tuscaloosa. ... Manning applauded the maturity of senior running back Smothers. "He's like a veteran. It feels like he's a 10-year All-Pro guy." ... Congratulate, Texas, on only two penalties for 12 yards. Of course, that officiating crew wasn't going to throw a flag for anything short of a homicide. Still, it was the cleanest game for the Longhorns since they were called for just two penalties for 10 yards in the CFP win at home over Clemson in 2024. ... The Longhorns rank tied for last with Kentucky in third down defense. Yikes. ... In baseball, Texas freshman pitcher Sam Cozart had right foot surgery this summer but is already playing catch and will be good to go in January. Second baseman Ethan Mendoza had shoulder surgery and is also sitting out fall drills. ... Saturday's game on ABC drew an audience of 14 million, making it the most-watched regular-season game in 10 years.

5. McMonster up front

I didn't know Bob McKay, who died last week at age 78, well. But I do know he was one of the best offensive linemen in UT history on a level with Jerry Sisemore, Dan Neil, Justin Blalock and Kelvin Banks Jr. And one of the biggest in his era. At 6-5, 236 pounds as a freshman, he was a behemoth and I mean that with the sincerest part of flattery. James Street dubbed him "Big Un" for a reason. ... Student manager Bill Hall said he probably texted McKay every day and remembers him as "one of the nicest human beings. If you were his friend, you were a friend for life." ... Running back teammate Ted Koy remembered McKay as the ultimate competitor on those wishbone days that included a 30-game win streak and two national titles. "If you just followed him," Koy said, "you were going in the right direction." ... McKay came from far, far, far West Texas at Crane, which played in Class AA and which the late Bill Little once wrote had a population of 37 people and 4,700 cattle. Darrell Royal showed up to recruit him, and McKay said, "It was like a parade. Everybody in town wanted to see him." ... Remember, he played on an offensive line that would be considered minuscule these days with teammates on the front like 200-pound Mike Dean. Texas' smallest offensive lineman now is right guard Brandon Baker at a very, uh, light 315 pounds. McKay was coming off shoulder surgery in May 1968. It was the next year that produced Texas' second national championship and was best remembered for the Game of the Century against Arkansas when Street connected with tight end Randy Peschel in one of the biggest pass receptions in school history. The fourth-down throw, which was called 53 Veer Pass, took the Longhorns to the Arkansas 13 and set up the game-winning touchdown and extra point. McKay was the first to reach Peschel downfield and lifted him off the ground, saying, "Nice catch, Pasquale." ... Of course, Texas sealed the national title with a 21-17 win over Notre Dame in the Cotton Bowl on Billy Dale's 1-yard run.

6. Things I think I know

I think the Cowboys redefined terrible until the Broncos re-redefined it Monday night. Their defenses can't stop anybody. Do NFL teams even practice tackling any more? ... I think I dig this NFL. Six games with a combined 60 points in Week 1. Sign me up. ... I think Josh Allen is my favorite quarterback. He deserves a Super Bowl. ... I think Bo Mascoe showed me a lot when the cornerback transfer from Rutgers shadowed Smith and held him without a catch in the fourth quarter on three targets. ... I think I know my fantasy football team is doomed now that I traded A.J. Brown after he was put on IR with a high ankle sprain. I know no one in the world cares about someone else's fantasy team but consider this venting and it's cheaper than a psychiatrist. ... I think I loved that the Rams lost Game 1 to the 49ers and destroys the nonsense LA might go undefeated. Kyle Shanahan is such a good coach. ... I think Mike Evans is such a stud. And a true Hall of Famer. He does not age.

7. Save Muny, please

Had a super time at Imagine Muny 5 at ACL last Thursday night. Good folks are doing everything in their power to preserve one of the most historic municipal golf courses in the country. Scotty Sayers, the longtime manager and friend of Ben Crenshaw, told the audience of about 2,200 that the Muny Conservancy committee is "optimistic" that the University of Texas will agree to keep open the 18-hold course in the heart of downtown that was one of the first golf courses in the South to desegregate and was a breeding ground for Crenshaw, Tom Kite, Mark Brooks and other greats instead of developing the land for commercial purposes. The fifth annual event raised $1 million, auctioning off things like Scottie Scheffler-signed Masters flags, Rory McIlroy-autographed wine bottles and rounds of golf at Pinehurst No. 2 before Ray Benson, Tanya Tucker and Jack Ingram sang. ... Sat with my wife Vicki at a table with Barbara Pruett, a former Texas State Champion, six-time Austin City Golf Champion and legendary instructor at the Barton Creek Golf Academy, and her daughter Paulette. Barbara told me she still plays nine holes every Sunday at Austin Country Club with her 93-year-old dad Roane, a Southwest Conference champion at Texas. Barbara is a Harvey Penick disciple who has taught four generations of Austin golfers. Oh, Paulette told me her five-time city champion father owns a career 22 holes-in-one. Crenshaw said he had his very first hole-in-one at age 10 at Muny and then had another two days later. Paulette's waiting on her first.

8. Scattershooting

While wondering whatever happened to Larry Coker, UTSA's first football coach.

9. On the couch

A double feature. Enjoyed the Hulu series called "Best Medicine." The comedy about an afflicted and socially awkward surgeon, who returns to practice at his former summer getaway community, isn't hilarious but offers enough laughs to make it very watchable. It renews for Season 2 next week. Gave it 6 ducks. ... Also recommend "Don't Say Good Luck," an entertaining movie starring Adam Sandler's daughter Sunny as a teenager dealing with her mother's terminal illness and her own complicated social life. She absolutely crushed it. Gave it 71/2 ducks.

Crazy prediction

Ohio State will go 11-1, win the Big Ten and reach the CFP championship game.

headline: GE Aerospace spending $225M on Niskayuna R&D center
hlead: GE Aerospace spending $225M on Niskayuna R&D center NISKAYUNA — GE Aerospace plans to spend $225 million over the next five years to expand and upgrade its research center in Niskayuna . “It’s an investment, not only in the facility and our research and development capability, but in our workforce as well,” Joseph Vinciquerra, general manager and senior executive director of research at GE Aerospace , told the Times Union in an exclusive phone interview. “GE Aerospace and the research center in Niskayuna really remain the front door to the GE Aerospace company from a technological perspective.” He continued: “The research center is the engine that is driving our next generation breakthroughs across artificial intelligence, autonomy, robotics, advanced materials manufacturing, hypersonic propulsion, and hybrid electric flight — just to name a few.”
text:
NISKAYUNA — GE Aerospace plans to spend $225 million over the next five years to expand and upgrade its research center in Niskayuna.

“It’s an investment, not only in the facility and our research and development capability, but in our workforce as well,” Joseph Vinciquerra, general manager and senior executive director of research at GE Aerospace, told the Times Union in an exclusive phone interview. “GE Aerospace and the research center in Niskayuna really remain the front door to the GE Aerospace company from a technological perspective.”

He continued: “The research center is the engine that is driving our next generation breakthroughs across artificial intelligence, autonomy, robotics, advanced materials manufacturing, hypersonic propulsion, and hybrid electric flight — just to name a few.”

GE Aerospace is headquartered in suburban Cincinnati and is essentially the last piece of the original General Electric Co. left standing after CEO H. Lawrence Culp Jr. split the company earlier this decade into three standalone companies that focus on the healthcare, energy, and aerospace sectors.

GE was founded in Schenectady in 1892 and opened its Niskayuna research center in 1950. All three GE spinoffs host their own labs and research space at the Niskayuna campus, designed to host large, multiday conferences and events, with places to walk and exercise, like a high-tech college campus.

Over the past few years, GE’s spinoffs have been investing hundreds of millions of dollars in their Capital Region facilities and hiring hundreds of new workers, many of them scientists.

GE Vernova, which employs hundreds of workers at GE’s historic manufacturing site in downtown Schenectady, making gas and wind turbine components and generators, also opened a second $110 million research campus in July on Balltown Road in Niskayuna, a short drive from the main research campus.

The GE Aerospace investment in its research and development facility is double that.

“The scale of this investment is very significant, and it’s really intended to modernize our R&D capabilities to keep the company itself competitive in the aerospace sector and to really be a national leader in industrial research and development for the aerospace industry,” Vinciquerra said. “This is all about keeping our leading-edge military and commercial jet engine R&D anchored in New York.”

Vinciquerra said both Empire State Development and Schenectady County Metroplex Development quickly put together financial incentive packages for the project, which had interest from other states.

“We couldn’t be more pleased with how quickly state and local government moved to help us make this investment possible,” Vinciquerra said. “This has been in the works (for a while), but New York state has just been fantastic, as has Schenectady County. They both are providing meaningful support.”

Empire State Development offered GE Aerospace $8.42 million in Excelsior Jobs Program tax credits, contingent on creating 75 jobs. Metroplex is providing a state sales tax break on construction materials used at the site.

“New York state has a bold legacy of innovation, built on the shoulders of big ideas and big investments by globally renowned companies like GE Aerospace,” Gov. Kathy Hochul said in a statement provided to the Times Union. “We want to ensure that the next generation of technological discoveries happens here, and today’s announcement demonstrates that our legacy is only getting stronger.”

The project also includes GE Aerospace expanding its workforce development ecosystem in the region.

“This investment includes ramping up our workforce partnerships with SUNY and other area trade schools and community colleges to really bolster that skilled trades training pipeline and be able to connect the investment directly with our local labor market,” Vinciquerra said.

Last year, the charitable arm of GE Aerospace brought its Next Engineers program to the Capital Region to help high school students become engineering students in college.

GE Aerospace had $13.3 billion in revenue during the second quarter of 2026. Its profit for the quarter was $2.8 billion. Its order backlog for the commercial aviation and defense markets stood at $210 billion back in July.

“We are facing unprecedented demand for our products and our services in GE Aerospace, and across the board we’re making critical investments to ensure that we can meet that demand,” Vinciquerra said when asked about the need to expand its Niskayuna research center. “We are in the thick of new technology development for our next-generation commercial engines.”

On the commercial side, that includes the new GE9X engine, which was designed specifically for the Boeing 777X, and the new RISE “open-fan” engine.

“On the defense side, there’s just an incredible amount of demand ranging from our traditional jet engines for combat aircraft, our helicopter engines, of course, and emerging technologies for the engines required for small (uncrewed) aircraft,” Vinciquerra said. “We continue the work that we’ve previously shared in areas such as hypersonics and advanced combustion technologies.”

Vinciquerra said the Niskayuna research center almost always hosts customers, and Culp, GE Aerospace’s CEO, is a “frequent” visitor.

“It’s all about the close partnership that we enjoy with our customers and the close working relationship that we value with our customers,” Vinciquerra said. “So, we always bring them into the research center so that we can pull back the curtain and show them the advanced technologies that we’re working on. I live in Clifton Park and just couldn’t be happier with the way things have unfolded. I think it’s good for the entire region.”

text:
Julia Demaree Nikhinson President Donald Trump speaks to the United Nations General Assembly, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, at the U.N. headquarters. 1

President Donald Trump delivered remarks before the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday in New York City, highlighting the United States' efforts to stop Iran from gaining a nuclear weapon, as well as his attempt to change the name of artificial intelligence.

While top U.N. officials urged for peace, Trump made the case for why the war with Iran was necessary.

"They were the bully of the Middle East, but they are the bully no more," the president said. "From the first day I entered the political arena, I have been unwavering. I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."

More than seven months into the conflict with Iran, he said he had a big question before him.

Julia Demaree Nikhinson UN General Assembly Trump UN General Assembly Trump 1

Trump wondered if he should strike a deal with Iran that would allow them to rebuild into a better country, or should he "annihilate the Islamic Republic" and never give them a chance to kill people again.

"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" he said. "But, I believe we'll make a deal right after the election because it doesn't make sense for them not to."

The remarks come as relations between the United States and many of its European allies are strained after they rejected Trump's request to aid in the war.

Trump talks Gaza and Iran

Yuki Iwamura UN General Assembly UN General Assembly 1

Trump spoke about his efforts to end the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, the excursion in Venezuela earlier this year and the ongoing war with Iran.

"One year ago, when I addressed the great leaders in this hall, the war in Gaza was still raging brutally," Trump said. "The hostages were still deep in Hamas tunnels, and there was no end in sight."

"But here, on the sidelines of the General Assembly, we took the first steps," he continued. "It changed everything. A few weeks later, we ended the war in Gaza, saving untold thousands of lives. We also brought home all remaining hostages, both living and dead."

U.N. Secretary-General gives farewell remarks

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres delivered his final address on Tuesday, detailing the issues the world faces and urging leaders to work together. He argued that the "fault-lines in our world are widening" and said the future will depend on how leaders step up on several key issues, including war and peace, wealth and inequality, climate chaos and artificial intelligence.

Guterres, who will step down in December after serving since 2017, called on leading nations to end global conflicts. Without naming Iran or Trump specifically, he said the conflicts in the Middle East were "cascading," saying "enough is enough."

While Guterres called on the leaders to improve the world going forward through diplomacy and peace, Trump used his time to explain why he believes it was necessary to intervene to thwart Iran's nuclear ambitions.

Trump said that when he retook office in January 2025, he immediately began negotiations with Iran, offering full economic cooperation if they gave up their nuclear program, but he said Iran refused. He said after military operations in the summer of 2025, he again offered Iran an opportunity to negotiate, which they refused.

The president has often criticized allied countries for not helping with the Iran military operation, which started in late February this year. He shared Tuesday that he hopes European leaders know Iran had made a missile capable of hitting Europe.

Trump argued that many presidents before him knew how much of a threat Iran would be but they chose to ignore it.

Yuki Iwamura UN General Assembly Trump UN General Assembly Trump 1

"After giving Iran every chance for a deal, I took action to ensure that neither the United States nor any nation would ever have to face such a nightmare," he said.

Trump thanked the United Nations Security Council for passing a resolution condemning Iran's "despicable terrorist attacks" on shipping vessels in the Strait of Hormuz following the initial attacks. Still, he called on the global leaders to be "equally united in maintaining pressure" on Iran.

With Trump facing pressure from Americans over continued high gas prices and increased disapproval over the war, Republicans are concerned the conflict will impact the 2026 midterm elections. The president said Tuesday that he thinks Iran is waiting to strike a deal until after the November elections.

U.S. cuts to the U.N. - and changes to AI

Throughout both of his terms, Trump has maintained an "America First" mentality when it comes to the United Nations.

During his first term, he worked through the U.N. Security Council to enact heavy sanctions on Iran, but also tried to scale back funding to agencies like the U.N. Population Fund. Trump also pulled the U.S. out of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization and the Paris Climate Accord.

Upon taking office for the second time, he also pulled the U.S. out of the U.N. Human Rights Council, as well as 31 other U.N entities as part of his administration's larger efforts to downsize government spending.

Yuki Iwamura UN General Assembly Trump UN General Assembly Trump 1

The U.S. had accumulated billions in unpaid debts to the U.N., which put the country at risk of losing voting privileges in the U.N. body. The administration recently paid $725 million to cover 2025 dues to maintain its standing with the U.N., Reuters reported earlier this month.

During his remarks Tuesday, Trump said NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte was a "great leader" and argued that the U.N. was "growing stronger than ever before."

He said that U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz has worked with many countries in the room to implement "the most sweeping U.N. reforms in history."

"We cut the U.N. budget for the first time ever, slashing it by 15% in 2026, and eliminating more than 4,000 positions from the U.N. bureaucracy," Trump said.

"The United Nations has great, great potential, I've said that for many years, but it must stop imposing the far left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected," he continued.

Trump also went on to talk about the U.S. efforts to dominate in the emerging artificial intelligence sector. He said that the United States will "totally reject" any attempts to make artificial intelligence into a "globalist scheme" for control.

The United States is in a race with China to maintain a lead in artificial intelligence development. During his remarks Tuesday, Trump said he was proposing a name change for AI.

He said artificial intelligence was being spoken of "so much now" and should "hereafter officially be called super intelligence." Trump said the word "artificial" makes the intelligence sound "fake."

"It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing. We have to be careful," he said. "In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports."

"From this point forward, all of the United States' documents - and hopefully the world's - will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to artificial," Trump continued. "So, it's super intelligence. In other words, welcome to the new world of super intelligence - S.I."

Trump went on to say that the country or group that wins the "super intelligence" race is the group that "wins." He said the U.S. is leading "by a lot" over China and "everyone else" and he wants to keep it that way.

Chinese President Xi Jinping will be making a state visit to Washington, D.C., starting Wednesday, where he will meet with Trump about the two countries' efforts to dominate the AI world.

While Trump is set to make the unusual move to meet Xi at the airport, experts don't expect the two to make some sort of large compromise about the emerging technology, ABC News reported.

text:
September 23rd, 2026 ( International Business Times News  - Delivered by  Newstex )

A smartphone displaying the Anthropic logo is shown in the foreground with the words Artificial Intelligence AI blurred in the arriere-plan in Tunis,Tunisia on July 11,2026. Getty Images

Anthropic and medical knowledge platform OpenEvidence are expanding an  AI-powered clinical decision-support service to physicians in about 100 countries, including several where doctors have limited access to specialist expertise, medical literature and other healthcare resources.

The initiative will provide a specialized version of OpenEvidence free to healthcare professionals in dozens of low- and middle-income countries, including Uganda, Angola, Sudan, Haiti and Mongolia. OpenEvidence already offers its platform free to clinicians in the United States and Europe. The service answers clinical questions using peer-reviewed medical research and treatment guidelines.

Anthropic will provide the underlying technology, while OpenEvidence will adapt the service to different regions and healthcare systems. Financial terms of the partnership were not disclosed.

OpenEvidence has already been working to tailor its technology for countries where disease patterns, diagnostic resources and available treatments can differ significantly from those in the United States and other wealthier markets.

In January, OpenEvidence partnered with the Rwanda Biomedical Center and nonprofit Resolve to Save Lives to evaluate its clinical decision-support technology in lower-resource settings. The project involved 45 Rwandan doctors and nurses who tested the system and provided feedback on how it could better reflect local clinical conditions, Resolve to Save Lives said at the time.

The company has also been working with healthcare organizations in Botswana, where differences in available treatments, diagnostic equipment and other resources can affect how medical information is used in practice.

The broader rollout includes countries where healthcare systems have been severely disrupted by war and humanitarian crises. Sudan, one of the countries covered by the initiative, has faced widespread damage to its healthcare system during more than three years of fighting.

As of April, 37% of health facilities across Sudan's 18 states were non-functional, while disease outbreaks and malnutrition were putting further pressure on the remaining system. The  World Health Organization said 21 million people lacked access to health services and it had verified 217 attacks on healthcare since the conflict began in April 2023.

Healthcare services have also been disrupted by fighting elsewhere. The  World Health Organization said the escalation of conflict across the Middle East since February has killed and injured civilians and health workers, damaged medical facilities and interrupted treatment for injuries and chronic illnesses. Disruptions to air and maritime routes have also affected the movement of medical equipment and humanitarian supplies.

Access to medical information does not always depend on hospital infrastructure. OpenEvidence founder Daniel Nadler said that even in places where medical facilities lack reliable electricity, most physicians have smartphones, giving them another way to access clinical information.

OpenEvidence is already widely used by doctors in the United States. American clinicians consulted the platform 42 million times in August alone, Nadler told Reuters. He said several hundred million Americans will have been treated during 2026 by a doctor who used OpenEvidence to help guide care.

The partnership comes as Anthropic expands its work in medicine and biological research beyond its general-purpose AI models. The company has established a laboratory in the San Francisco Bay Area to conduct physical biology experiments as part of its push into life sciences and drug research. Anthropic has also developed Claude Science software and acquired Coefficient Bio.

The growing use of AI in medicine has also brought scrutiny over how such systems perform outside the environments in which they were developed. One issue is whether tools trained largely on information from wealthier countries adequately reflect differences in diseases, treatments and medical resources elsewhere.

text:
September 24th, 2026 ( Techdirt  - Delivered by  Newstex )

from the narrative-violation-in-progress dept

Over the last few years, it has become accepted knowledge that the internet - mainly social media and, lately, AI tools - was damaging the mental health of kids and increasing the suicide rate among that demographic. To hear the media and politicians talk about it, this was the biggest issue on the planet and we had to do basically everything possible to block social media (and AI) from kids.

Of course, the narrative  was always bullshit. While there had been an uptick in suicide rates among teens between 2010 and 2020, they were way below the rates in the 80s and 90s. And by the time Jonathan Haidt's 'moral panic in a book' came out blaming social media for teen mental health problems, the data already didn't support his claims, as I pointed out in my review of the book right after it came out.

In that review of the book, I highlighted that while suicide rates among teens had ticked up in the US, they had actually declined in many other countries - including France, Spain, New Zealand, and elsewhere - despite plenty of social media usage in those countries. Similarly, the data on mental health issues was clouded by (1) much more openness to talking about mental health, and (2) importantly, new guidance under the Affordable Care Act that mandated increased screening for depression in adolescent girls, while simultaneously instructing clinicians to record suicidal ideation differently than in the past, which resulted in a massive uptick in such numbers.

And now the narrative violation continues, as  the latest CDC survey data shows that mental health concerns among teens have been declining since their 2021 peak (i.e., as we were coming out of the worst of the COVID crisis).

Continuing a trend  first observed in 2023, teenagers surveyed at high schools across the country in 2025 reported improvements in several key measures, including persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness, serious thoughts of suicide and attempting suicide in the last year.

Some might argue that this is due to the work of Haidt and politicians banning social media for kids, but the data doesn't seem to show that at all.

Thirty-six percent of teenagers said that they used social media every hour or more, a similar percentage to what was seen in 2023, when the data was first reported.

And while this survey doesn't track AI usage, we know from other research that  a large majority of teens now use AI chatbots, with roughly three in ten using them daily.

This does not mean, of course, that we can declare victory. There are still, clearly, plenty of teens dealing with mental health challenges.

But the data show that many teenagers, especially girls and teenagers who identify as lesbian, gay or bisexual, are still struggling. Thirty-three percent of high school students reported persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness in the last 12 months, down from a peak of 42 percent in 2021. Fourteen percent of teenagers reported that they had seriously considered attempting suicide, down from 22 percent in 2021.

As  actual experts have been pointing out for years, the reality around mental health and suicidal ideation is extremely complicated and not fully understood. But, over and over again it seems that the approach recommended by actual experts is not blanket bans on technology or simply 'blaming' anything, but rather better efforts at identifying those going through mental health challenges while simultaneously making more mental health resources available to all who need them.

But, the narrative is the narrative. Hell, it was just weeks ago that a judge in New Mexico  took it as irrefutably proven that social media was damaging to kids' mental health. Does anyone get to go back and show him the latest data suggesting that maybe something else was driving this? Or do we just keep treating the narrative as fact?

This is what I've been saying for years: when we misdiagnose the problem and blame the wrong thing, the 'solutions' we get are not solutions at all. Indeed, they could be making the problem worse by not actually putting in place the tools and resources to help those in need while, simultaneously, doing real damage to groups that rely on internet communities for their own mental health support.

I'd like to think that as more data like this comes out, further debunking Haidt's narrative, we could get back to a serious discussion about how to actually help kids who are struggling. But I fear the easy comfort of a moral panic is too strong a pull for people to give it up that quickly.

headline: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta -led alliance - how businesses could make it work
hlead: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta -led alliance - how businesses could make it work When a swarm of AI agents, many autonomously provisioned by other poorly governed AI agents, escaped OpenAI 's labs and stole information from servers belonging to another company (Hugging Face), many experts viewed the incident as a major tipping point in cybersecurity and AI cyber capabilities. (To what extent are models now resourceful enough to engage in self-directed harm?) OpenAI referred to the incident as " unprecedented ." It was the first AI-directed  attack of its nature to go viral across mainstream headlines, and it wasn't long before reports of other agents-gone-wild made headlines as well. The most recent of these reports involved three companies that were inadvertently attacked by Google Gemini agents . Also: How OpenAI 's agent escaped: A series of preventable events
text:
ZDNET's key takeaways

Okta, AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and others form an AI agent security coalition.

The Alliance offers a blueprint for companies seeking visibility, control, and governance of agents.

AI agents need the equivalent of a kill switch to expeditiously terminate suspicious behavior.

When a swarm of AI agents, many autonomously provisioned by other poorly governed AI agents, escaped OpenAI's labs and stole information from servers belonging to another company (Hugging Face), many experts viewed the incident as a major tipping point in cybersecurity and AI cyber capabilities. (To what extent are models now resourceful enough to engage in self-directed harm?)

OpenAI referred to the incident as "unprecedented." It was the first AI-directed  attack of its nature to go viral across mainstream headlines, and it wasn't long before reports of other agents-gone-wild made headlines as well. The most recent of these reports involved three companies that were inadvertently attacked by Google Gemini agents.

Also: How OpenAI's agent escaped: A series of preventable events

Significant controversy has ensued.

In one corner are the inventors of AI themselves, saying that the time has come to take a breather from AI innovation in order to get the technology under control. You'd think they should know. For example, OpenAI sounded the alarm that a swarm of potentially malicious AI agents is only months away from wreaking havoc.

In the opposite corner is US President Trump posting to his Truth Social network that "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX."

In between are all the businesses and consumers getting whipsawed between the two points of view and trying to figure out what to do next.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET's parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Also: 'Sophisticated' AI swarm attacks are months away, OpenAI warns

Two big questions are arising out of this conversation. First, what can be done over the short and long term to get the technology under control? Second, how can defenders best enable themselves for immediate intervention once suspicious activity is detected?

With the goal of helping businesses answer those two questions and to set the stage for world-class governance and management of their agentic estates, several companies, including Okta, Google, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Salesforce, have joined forces to form the Blueprint Alliance.

The Alliance was announced this week at Okta's annual Oktane conference.

4 questions every business must answer

In its first blueprint for agentic visibility, control, and governance, the Alliance centered on four questions that all businesses should be able to answer for themselves:

Where are my agents?

What can they do?

What are they doing?

How do I respond?

According to recent research conducted by LastPass (not a member of the Alliance), 92% of business admins say AI is already in use across their organization, but only 27% have an enforced AI governance program. Okta's research reports similar statistics, finding that 92% of organizations use autonomous agents, but only 34% secure those agents with the same rigor as humans.

Meanwhile, Gartner's research paints an even bleaker picture, finding that only 13% of organizations believe they have the right AI agent governance in place. In other words, most organizations probably don't know the answer to some or all of the above questions. The fourth question is particularly important because of the degree to which problematic agents working at machine speed have shortened the response window.

Also: AI just broke your career ladder - here are 6 new ways to the top

As Picus Security associate security research engineer Umut Bayram told ZDNET,  "In the AI era, organizations can't respond to attacks that unfold in minutes with processes that take days. Attackers are already operating at machine speed, and security teams need to be able to respond at that pace."

In fairness, not all anomalous agent activity is malicious. Here's another scenario that demands an immediate response: a well-intentioned agent enters an infinite loop, resulting in excessive billing for LLM access. At machine speeds, such a loop could burn through an entire organization's AI budget in the blink of an eye. The sooner such an agent is disabled, the better for the bottom line.

The best defenses are scenario-specific

Of course, in the cybersecurity world, speed has always been essential - but never more so than now. And given how defenders may only have minutes or seconds to respond once they've been alerted to anomalous agent activity, what should be their weapon of choice?

To be clear: There is no silver bullet. As with all cybersecurity, the best defenses are scenario-specific and will involve layers of precautionary measures, some that focus on visibility into agentic activities, and others that tune the security postures of our computers and networks to emerging agentic behaviors and patterns.

Also: Even an AI cost-management vendor can lose control of its agent spending

For example, businesses must be prepared to defend against malicious agents of unknown origin as well as internally provisioned agents that, for whatever reasons, stray from their mandates. Unlike robotic automations that deliver highly deterministic outcomes (they do exactly as they were programmed to do), agents are probabilistic to the extent that their underlying models afford them the agency to take matters into their own hands.

When mere seconds can make the difference between the life and death of your systems or even your business, the ideal weapon of choice would be some sort of kill switch - something like the big red button on an escalator. When in doubt, neutralize the agent first, ask questions later.

What is a kill switch?

In an effort to put organizations on the right path, the new alliance published six operational principles, one of which states that "every agent needs an immediate kill switch to suspend or terminate operations, with a clear path to restore function." But, practically speaking, what exactly is a kill switch, and who might have access to one?

It depends.

For example, in the case of OpenAI's attack on Hugging Face, the agents belonged to OpenAI. Presumably, if OpenAI had the right governance controls in place (it didn't), it might have detected that its own agents were engaging in suspicious behavior, and then someone at OpenAI with access to a kill switch could have pulled the plug. What about Hugging Face? Did it have access to a kill switch? Probably not to the extent that OpenAI did, since it was OpenAI's agents that led the attack. But what if an attack on a victim like Hugging Face involved the theft of its credentials to some online service or business application?

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now - but many get no time to upskill

Today, one of the more coveted credentials that cybercriminals like to steal are OAuth tokens. These are a type of credential that gives one application (e.g. Slack) access rights to read and update another application (e.g. Google Drive) on behalf of a specific user. In that context, the Google-issued OAuth token that gives Slack the access it needs to work with a specific user's Google Drive is essentially a proxy for the user's Google ID and password.

In a scenario that involves an agent (friendly or malicious) using an OAuth credential (stolen or not) to interact with a sensitive resource, a neutralization of that token (known as "token revocation") would essentially amount to a kill switch.

In other words, for certain types of attacks, the victim might have a kill switch at their disposal. And that same option applies to the organization's own agents because, if they're doing it right, then their own agents are also using OAuth tokens to access all of their systems of record in order to do what agents do best (autonomously complete tasks that often require access to multiple systems).

The role of OAuth tokens

When it comes to granting one application access to another, consumers are already familiar with the typical OAuth experience (though they may not know it's technically referred to as an OAuth workflow). In earlier days, consumers would enter their Gmail user IDs and passwords directly into Apple Mail or Outlook to send and receive email through their preferred email client. Today, however, Google offers a more secure alternative that relies on OAuth tokens. Instead of supplying your Gmail user ID and password to a third-party email client like Apple Mail on your iPhone (a highly insecure practice), Gmail pops up a consent dialog that, once approved by the user, grants a Gmail access token to their email client. From that point on, the email client should be able to send and receive emails without requiring repeated grant requests.

However, should the user lose their iPhone and, as an extra precaution, want to revoke that token, the process is a bit more complicated: it requires a visit to a Google web page where users can manage tokens they've already issued.

Also: Why Microsoft won't send you SMS texts for login anymore

As consumers start to deploy agents that interact with all of the services they use (Gmail, Google Drive, Amazon shopping, social media, music streaming, etc.), they are not only likely to encounter many more Oauth workflows, but they will need to familiarize themselves with each service's token revocation process as a matter of their personal operational security practices.

For businesses, however, especially ones that rely on an identity management solution like those offered by Okta, Microsoft, and Ping, those same tokens should be managed in a way that centralize token issuance and management into a single system where it's the IT managers who not only have access to the proverbial kill switches (the power to revoke any token that's connected to any human or agentic-powered integration), but also, in answer to the "Where are my agents?" question, offer visibility and control over the organization's entire agentic estate.

However, to facilitate those kill switches and that centralized visibility and control, a new extension to the underlying OAuth standard was needed, allowing the central IdP (identity provider) to take responsibility for OAuth workflows and management when AI agents are involved. It was just in this past year that the open standard agentic-sensitive extension -known as the IETF's Identity Assertion Authorization Grant (IAAG) - fell into place, thanks in large part to the work done by Okta director of identity standards Aaron Parecki.

Implementing the standard

But it's one thing for people like Parecki and others, including IAAG co-author Brian Campbell (Ping Identity), to author a new standard and to achieve standard consensus at the Internet Engineering Task Force. It's another for that standard to be baked into the various IdPs in a way that facilitates the provision of a readily accessible kill switch in the event that the answer to the third question is "something they shouldn't be doing."

At the Oktane conference, Okta executives gave customers a demonstration of how its identity and security solutions rely on the new standard to provide IT managers and CISOs with visualizations that, in addition to answering the four questions, also empower them (or even an agent working on their behalf) to take action.

Also: Don't let an AI chatbot pick your password, ever

For example, the screenshot below depicts how a single Claude-based agent has been afforded access to Slack, Salesforce, Atlassian, and GitHub through two separate agent gateways.

Under the hood, OAuth isn't just giving Claude access to those applications. It's also controlling the degree of access, an important nuance to the idea of a kill switch. For example, a kill switch that fully revokes a token would essentially deprovision an agent's access to a back-end application such as Salesforce. But another type of kill switch could simply revoke certain permissions to interact with Salesforce.

Deprovisioning demonstration

"There are actually two scenarios here," Okta chief product officer Ely Kahn told ZDNET. "There's the one where your own agents start to exhibit weird behavior, and you have to kill them [the nuclear option] just to stop that behavior before it gets out of control. But then there's another scenario where you can just put a new guardrail in place. For example, a new guardrail that prevents the exfiltration of certain data or just a change in the permissions afforded to the agent."

During Okta CEO Todd McKinnon's conference keynote, Oktane attendees got a glimpse of what that deprovisioning looks like in practice. As soon as a Claude agent was asked to forward confidential information from Salesforce to an employee's personal email address, another agent detected the prohibited behavior, deprovisioned the first agent's access to Salesforce (revoked its token), notified the agent's human owner that Salesforce access was now denied, and sent a message via Slack to the IT department including any details that would be useful in terms of a remedy or restoration of access.

Also: Your AI vendor could land you in legal hot water

Speaking to the need for speed described by Picus Security's Bayram, the entire process was completed in a matter of seconds, long before any human could have assembled a response.

In his keynote, McKinnon also pointed out that IdPs like Okta can't necessarily address every aspect of the Blueprint Alliance's blueprint and that some of the non-identity-based telemetry that helps to determine what an agent is doing must come from other sources. That said, Okta also showed two other tools that could be valuable to businesses looking to gain control of their agentic estate. One of these - Shadow AI Agent Discovery for Endpoints - helps organizations discover unsanctioned "shadow" AI agents roaming company networks.

Another tool - Okta Identity Threat Protection - aggregates risk intelligence from other agentic risk detection solutions (CrowdStrike, Zscaler, SentinelOne, Palo Alto Networks, etc.) into a single view for human- or agentically driven remediation decisions.

text:
I am currently reading Imagine It Forward by Beth Comstock, former vice chair of General Electric. Comstock talks about the power (and necessity) of change, which commonly involves tension, risk and failure. Yet, change is absolutely essential for personal and professional success. I've been thinking about the current waves of change in our veterinary profession. Most notable in my day-to-day work life has been the introduction and rapid development of artificial intelligence.

Life as a new graduate (we're talking the first three-plus years out of school) was tough, and this is a universal experience across our profession. I spent a minimum of 40 hours per week in the clinic and a significant amount of my "off" time working from home. Working from home included completing patient charts, interpreting diagnostics, calling owners with results and electronically documenting our phone conversations. Most recent graduates also have shifts where they work alone, without other consulting doctors in the hospital. I spent a significant amount of time studying X-rays and lab results, wondering if it was appropriate to wake a colleague to discuss a case.

I am fortunate to work in a progressive environment where change is welcomed and embraced. In April 2024, our company announced we were transitioning to brand-new software that would eventually have AI-integrated capabilities. It was scary. Staff panicked, and old systems were disrupted. Our leadership chose to move forward, and this was the single most transformative workplace decision I have experienced in my professional life.

Artificial intelligence has revolutionized our practice in one primary capacity: medical record-keeping. Doctors and veterinary nurses have tablets that we carry throughout the day to audio-record physical examination findings, client conversations, diagnostic findings and treatment plans. I also audio-dictate surgical reports after my patients are settled outside the operating room. At the end of a patient interaction, our AI-integrated software summarizes the audio input and creates a "sample" version of the medical record, which I can subsequently edit and sign.

I am spending approximately one-tenth of the time on medical record-keeping that I was spending last year.

Additionally, new professional AI services are becoming readily available. I recently had a 3-year-old golden retriever who was vomiting, and his family was concerned he might have ingested a piece of cloth. On physical examination, the patient was comfortable on abdominal palpation, and his intestines palpated soft and uniform in size. I submitted his X-rays for an AI read with the question: Are we concerned this dog has a gastrointestinal obstruction? The AI algorithm had a high degree of certainty that the patient did not have an intestinal obstruction, and AI was correct. The clients were reassured, and I was reassured about the recommendations I had already provided.

These tools do not replace our physical examination findings, years of education or clinical reasoning. Instead, they can provide another resource when we are working a solo shift or simply looking for another perspective.

I am confident that AI will never replace the job of a veterinarian. I am still going to walk into the exam room, examine my patient and build a relationship with my clients. I am going to recommend tailored testing and interpret those diagnostics based on my training and experience. The difference is my time.

Instead of spending so much time outside of work charting, I am now able to spend time with my own animals and enjoy more simple pleasures of everyday life. Now I am able to show up for my clients and patients better than ever before.

Beth Comstock says, "Be where the world is going." A growing number of folks in the veterinary world are taking this to heart. It is very reasonable to imagine a world where artificial intelligence is a larger part of our days as medical professionals. Perhaps, rather than making our jobs obsolete, these tools will allow us to spend more of our time doing what we became veterinarians to do: caring for animals, supporting their families and practicing the medicine we love.

Dr. Kelsey Dobesh grew up in Santa Fe and is a fourth-generation veterinarian at Smith Veterinary Hospital. Dobesh graduated from St. Michael's High School and attended Colorado State University to study agricultural business and animal science. She has been practicing veterinary medicine for five years.

headline: A Look Inside the Project Taurus Special Meeting
hlead: A Look Inside the Project Taurus Special Meeting Nearly six hours into a nine-hour special city council meeting to appeal the decision to approve Project Taurus, a controversial proposed data center to be built on Garden of the Gods Road, tensions reached a breaking point. The hearing was intended to be the final decision on the project's sixth re-evaluation appeal. Anticipating a massive turnout, the meeting was held in the Pikes Peak Center for the Performing Arts and public comments were limited to 120 speakers per side after the previous meeting on the matter did not conclude until well past 11 p.m. For the first several hours of the hearing, things went as usual: appellants brought in expert testimony on potential damages to decibel levels and Jason Green , CEO of AI real estate developer Raeden, presented arguments as to why the company's plan for the data center met city standards.
text:
Nearly six hours into a nine-hour special city council meeting to appeal the decision to approve Project Taurus, a controversial proposed data center to be built on Garden of the Gods Road, tensions reached a breaking point. The hearing was intended to be the final decision on the project's sixth re-evaluation appeal. Anticipating a massive turnout, the meeting was held in the Pikes Peak Center for the Performing Arts and public comments were limited to 120 speakers per side after the previous meeting on the matter did not conclude until well past 11 p.m.

For the first several hours of the hearing, things went as usual: appellants brought in expert testimony on potential damages to decibel levels and Jason Green, CEO of AI real estate developer Raeden, presented arguments as to why the company's plan for the data center met city standards.

Following argumentation came community comments, first from those in favor of the project. Most speakers during this section told the same story. They were retired, or successful business owners, or had some military background, or had a personal vested interest in the project - or, for most, all four. Their story was also quite similar. "Colorado Springs is open for business," they cried, neither knowing which companies would occupy the space nor understanding the still-unclear military connection to the project. Far outnumbering them were a wide variety of attendees holding signs that showed messages like "CUT THE BULL." Most attendees were notably hostile toward speakers for the "pro" side and booed each person as soon as their allotted two minutes expired.

Though the "pro" section was long, the "against" section was magnitudes longer and lasted nearly three hours.Resident after resident stood at the podiums and expressed their frustration with the city's legislative body for repeatedly ignoring their comments in the months leading up to this hearing. A 14-year-old boy even showed communication between himself and Green in which Green doubted the boy's age, dismissing his concerns as "catfishing."

Wendy Jerado, a community member at the meeting, did not immediately rise or raise her hand when her name was called. After speaking with the nearest law enforcement officer, she was escorted to the podium, claiming she was skipped. Jerado refused to return to her seat, and police officers eventually ushered her away from the podium, despite the consensus in the room being to let her talk. Instead of even acknowledging Jerado's presence, the City Council ignored her and kept reading names to come to the podium. Yet no one did. No one wanted to take Jerado's two minutes away from her, even if she didn't rise when she was called. Moments later, she was handed a megaphone, and she began repeatedly questioning city council members about why she was skipped from the back of the room. Immediately, attendees around her began standing and yelling at the stage. In a matter of seconds, most of the room was either shouting at the councillors or gathered in a crowd around Colorado Springs Police Department officers as they tased a man standing near Jerado who had thrown a punch at a cop and was attempting to shield her.

Jerado made her way back to the podium, where she asked again why she wasn't allowed to comment. Looming over the scene from a raised box, Green stood up and simply stared at her. Several other attendees joined her in yelling at both Green and the City Council. I was at the meeting and witnessed everything presented here firsthand. The dichotomy was clear.Regardless of whether attendees had followed proper decorum, this much was true: those with power and money stood above those without.

Jerado and two others were arrested after the meeting concluded hours later. After such a clear display of discontent, Colorado Springs City Council decided to save themselves. This was made abundantly clear when council members questioned city staff about concerns raised by the appellants and community members that city ordinances about noise levels and power regulations were unsatisfactory. Councilman Ronald Rainey introduced a motion to postpone the decision until April 13, 2027, because the city "clearly isn't ready" to decide. It passed 7-2.

Interestingly, another motion was filed to delay the decision until before City Council elections on April 6, 2027. This motion failed 3-9.The City Council knew they had to buy more time, but didn't want their decision on Project Taurus to impact their re-election campaigns. Their job security mattered more than their constituents' desires to make a decision already.

But here's the thing. The meeting was a semi-judicial hearing to decide whether the appeal had room to stand on. It wasn't deciding if Project Taurus would be built at all, which would likely be several years in the future.What it became, however, was a desperate plea to remove outside money from local politics. Project Taurus comes with a hefty one-billion-dollar price tag, and the amended project outline offers few real consequences if Raeden violates city standards. Raeden is a California-based data center development company that is only seven years old. It is already involved in two legal disputes in 2026 over other projects across the country. The specific companies planning to use Project Taurus are unclear because Raeden has signed non-disclosure agreements with them.

To the Colorado Springs community, all of this looks like a random out-of-state company has co-opted the government, more concerned with an arbitrary AI race and scramble for precious data center revenue than it is with the well-being of its own residents. When Wendy Jerado asked why she couldn't speak, council members plainly stared at her. When Jason Green looked down at her with pity in his eyes, they stayed seated. The meeting was a gross display of the city council's self-interest and their decision to postpone the hearing until they wouldn't have to face the consequences of their actions only proves that. They were never going to decide on the issue if it impacted the elections. The verdict doesn't matter because the community's expression of frustration proved something much more powerful: the city council is terrified of them and their ballots.

Nick Smela

headline: Inside the AI-Powered Mortal Kombat II Workout That Got This 30-Something a Shredded Six-Pack in 12 Weeks
hlead: Inside the AI-Powered Mortal Kombat II Workout That Got This 30-Something a Shredded Six-Pack in 12 Weeks As Ludi Lin hurled a fireball across the big screen at the razor-hat-wielding Kung Lao in Mortal Kombat II, Anthony Truong sat up in his seat. "As soon as I saw Liu Kang, and I saw how big his arms were," Truong said, "I said, 'OK, now I need to dial in. I want to look like a superhero now.'" Truong had already started to think about dialing in for his health, with his eyes on lowering his resting heart rate. But that's the kind of goal that guys often feel like they should pursue. Looking like Lin in MK2? That's the kind of want that got Truong into the gym and locked in at mealtimes. And that inspiration worked: Three months after munching popcorn in the theater, Truong looked every bit the superhero. He'd dropped 10 pounds, a DEXA scan clocked his body fat at 10.3 percent, and he's sporting a blocky, chiseled six-pack.
text:
As Ludi Lin hurled a fireball across the big screen at the razor-hat-wielding Kung Lao in Mortal Kombat II, Anthony Truong sat up in his seat.

"As soon as I saw Liu Kang, and I saw how big his arms were," Truong said, "I said, 'OK, now I need to dial in. I want to look like a superhero now.'"

Truong had already started to think about dialing in for his health, with his eyes on lowering his resting heart rate. But that's the kind of goal that guys often feel like they should pursue. Looking like Lin in MK2? That's the kind of want that got Truong into the gym and locked in at mealtimes.

And that inspiration worked: Three months after munching popcorn in the theater, Truong looked every bit the superhero. He'd dropped 10 pounds, a DEXA scan clocked his body fat at 10.3 percent, and he's sporting a blocky, chiseled six-pack.

What makes Truong's transformation relatable for every MJ guy is that he did it all with workouts that lasted just an hour each, from a plan he fine-tuned to match his lifestyle with an AI chatbot. And he was able to stick to high-protein macros while eating dinners that weren't always "diet-friendly," dialing in the rest of the day to keep his evening meals delicious, satisfying, and motivating. Here's how Truong transformed into Liu Kang, and the diet strategies and workouts that got him there in just 12 weeks.

Want the latest fitness advice and workouts to tackle any adventure? Sign up for our Blueprint newsletter.

Balancing Fat-loss Macros with Mom's Home Cooking

While he was burning to look like Lin, Truong didn't want to give up his home-cooked Vietnamese favorites.

Most nights, the finance worker heads to his mother's house for dinner, which is a short drive from his own home in Denver. Not only is the evening meal valuable family time, but Truong's mother also cooks Vietnamese food that he describes as "bomb": Hu tieu, pho, stir-fries, or braised pork or fish with rice. Truong still wanted to bond with his mom (and wolf down all these delicious dishes), but also needed to find a way to shave off the fat to look like he could chuck a ball of flame.

This is similar to the situation facing many family guys trying to get lean: While we may not all have mom's home cooking to look forward to, we may still need to eat a family dinner with the kids (including kid-friendly, not fat loss-friendly, fare). If you don't want to cook two different meals and punk out on family dinner time, you've got to adjust the rest of the day, when you do have control.

That's exactly what Truong did. Depending on what he'd be eating at the family meal that night, he'd tweak his daily calories and macros to match. At breakfast, he'd normally eat some oatmeal, a few scrambled eggs, and three ounces of salmon from his job's cafeteria. But on days when pork was on the dinner menu, Truong says, "my fat's already exploded for the day." So he'd dial back the salmon to adjust.

Lunch was the same drill: Most days he'd have six to seven ounces of grilled chicken, a portion of rice, and some broccoli. Boring, sure, but functional to help keep the full day in check...and easy to stomach when you know a delicious dinner's in the works. If dinner was carb-heavy, he could dial back the rice. And if dinner left his daily protein lacking, he could supplement in the evening with some fat-free Greek yogurt or a protein shake.

The lesson for MJ guys: Figure out which parts of your daily nutrition you can control, and adjust those parts of the day to account for the meals where you're not at the helm. If you know you're headed for a work dinner, dial back the fat content at lunch. Know it's pasta night for the kids? Skimp a little on carbs at midday.

And if there's a day where things go haywire, don't punish yourself mentally or with gobs of extra cardio, Truong says.

"Don't let one cookie turn into a 3,000-calorie gorge-fest," he advises, " it's consistency over time that matters. That single cookie is a drop in the bucket over a whole week or two."

Related: Brad Pitt's 'Fight Club' Workout: Inside the Most Talked-About Celebrity Transformation of All Time

Using AI to Tweak and Hone his MK2 Workout

With early family dinners and an hour-long commute each way, Truong wanted to make every minute of his workouts count towards his goals. He was already a consistent exerciser and was only 10 pounds away from his goal. So he put what he was already doing into ChatGPT and Claude, and asked for help making tweaks.

text:
Q: After reading your article on lipoprotein(a), I wanted to share my experience. In February of 2024, I thought I had indigestion. When antacids did not relieve the symptoms, I went to the emergency room and was diagnosed with a mild heart attack. My weight is normal; I exercise often and have well-controlled blood pressure and slightly elevated cholesterol levels. My primary care doctor did not have me on statins. A heart catheterization revealed that I had four major blockages in my coronary arteries, and I had a quadruple bypass operation. My doctor said I was the last patient he would have expected to have heart problems. The cardiologist I have seen since my surgery did not test my Lp(a) levels. After seeing a news segment, I requested testing. My level was 345 nmol/L! Although there is currently no treatment available, I believe testing is important. Because of the possible hereditary link, I urged my children to be tested. Their levels are very low. Fortunately, my heart is not damaged, but I am aware of potential risks. Keep urging your readers to be tested.

A: We are shocked that your cardiologist did not order a test for Lp(a). The American College of Cardiology recently updated its guidelines and now recommends that everyone be tested for this risk factor at least once. Your level was extremely high and might well explain why you had a heart attack and clogged arteries.

A new clinical trial of the drug pelacarsen to lower Lp(a) yielded disappointing results. It worked to reduce Lp(a) but did not prevent heart attacks and strokes.

There are other ways to manage this risk. You can learn more about aspirin, niacin, PCSK9 inhibitors and diet in our "eGuide to Cholesterol Control & Heart Health." This online resource may be found under the Health eGuides tab at PeoplesPharmacy.com.

Q: I use NasalCrom, aka cromolyn nasal spray, several times a day. It helps a lot at night. Corticosteroid sprays and antihistamines are out due to dry eye problems. I also use nasal strips at night. The combination of NasalCrom and the nasal strips helps keep my nasal passages open better than anything else I've ever tried.

A: Cromolyn is a mast cell stabilizer. Mast cells pump out histamine and other inflammatory compounds when they detect allergens. This old-fashioned over-the-counter nose spray works best preventively, several times a day.

Q: After my knee surgery, I was put on Eliquis to prevent clots. I immediately had a reaction to it: severe, explosive diarrhea and extremely low blood pressure. It would take me 2 liters of fluid and electrolytes every morning to be functional. When I reached out to my surgeon's office, I did not receive a response. So, I researched what other surgeons prescribed -- baby aspirin. I took myself off Eliquis and took the aspirin with food. It took me six weeks of yogurt and fermented foods to get my gut back to normal. I looked up the side effects of Eliquis and found diarrhea listed, but as a rare side effect. When I told my surgeon about it at my next checkup, he supported my decision to swap it out for baby aspirin instead.

A: Surgeons often prescribe apixaban (Eliquis) after hip or knee replacement to prevent dangerous blood clots from forming. But some orthopedic surgeons are embracing low-dose aspirin (81 milligrams) for this purpose.

A study in the Journal of Arthroplasty (July 15, 2026) demonstrated that aspirin was as good as "potent anticoagulants" following joint replacement surgery.

headline: Walmart Embraces New Digital Shelf Labels, Not Dynamic Pricing: 'We Won't Do It,' CEO Vows
hlead: Walmart Embraces New Digital Shelf Labels, Not Dynamic Pricing: 'We Won't Do It,' CEO Vows DSLs will be in every store and Sam's Club by year's end, but John Furner says AI will never tweak prices based on each shopper's personal data, including income and purchase history. Yes, Walmart will soon have digital shelf labels in all 4,600-plus stores nationwide as well as its 600 members-only Sam's Club warehouses. And, yes, the company has in place the artificial intelligence and wireless technology that can rapidly raise or lower prices on those labels through a centralized system.
text:
DSLs will be in every store and Sam's Club by year's end, but John Furner says AI will never tweak prices based on each shopper's personal data, including income and purchase history.

Yes, Walmart will soon have digital shelf labels in all 4,600-plus stores nationwide as well as its 600 members-only Sam's Club warehouses.

And, yes, the company has in place the artificial intelligence and wireless technology that can rapidly raise or lower prices on those labels through a centralized system.

Taken together, the world's largest retailer now has the tools that make it possible to roll out dynamic pricing, the increasingly common practice of changing prices in real time based on market demand, supply levels, or even a customer's income and shopping history.

But chief executive officer John Furner wants Walmart's millions of shoppers to know one thing: "We won't do it."

"For more than 50 years, our pricing principle has been Every Day Low Prices (EDLP): low, consistent prices you can count on without guessing whether Monday or Tuesday is the better day to shop or wondering if someone else is getting a better price than you," Furner wrote in an earnest 600-word letter posted online Friday afternoon. "Using someone's income, shopping history or moment of need to charge them more would violate the EDLP promise our business model is built on."

The unexpected pledge, addressed to "customers and members," comes as Walmart puts the finishing touches on its plan to install digital shelf labels in all of its U.S. stores by the end of the year.

But shoppers need not worry that AI will soon be sizing up how badly they might want an item and how much they'd probably be willing to pay.

"We don't set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won't," Furner wrote. "Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won't change the price."

The retail giant says the new electronic displays actually serve a purpose far more mundane than the manipulations of dynamic pricing. DSLs render physical price tags all but obsolete, freeing employees from the time-consuming job of removing and attaching new ones. More importantly, the digital tech helps ensure that shelf prices match the amount customers are charged at checkout.

Furner said his vow also applies to Sparky, Walmart's AI-powered shopping assistant. Information consumers enter into the tool will not be used to jack up prices or withhold cheaper alternatives.

"We price the product, not the person," he wrote.

Furner's decision to publicly declare how Walmart will and won't use AI and digital pricing technology comes at a challenging time for the retailer, which has been grappling with slower growth as inflation-weary consumers remain cautious about spending.

Yet the retail giant continues to lean into its EDLP mantra. In July, as escalating food prices showed signs of straining household budgets, Walmart rolled back prices on a selection of groceries, including ground beef, cutting the price from $6.74 to $5.94 a pound. The national average price hit a record high of $6.92 a pound in August.

Furner's letter reinforces the low-price commitment that has been the foundation of Walmart's business for more than 60 years and countless pricing tools, from ink stampers and price guns to bar codes.

"Technology will keep changing," Furner said. "Our responsibility to earn your trust and help you save money and live better won't."
