headline: Couples are using a viral AI agent to do their emotional labor. It's been helpful - and chaotic.
highlight: Instinct's new "Trusted Person" feature allows couples' AI agents to interact with each other, marketed as a way to reduce mental load.
hlead: Couples are using a viral AI agent to do their emotional labor. It's been helpful - and chaotic. Instinct's new "Trusted Person" feature allows couples' AI agents to interact with each other, marketed as a way to reduce mental load. • Instinct 's new "Trusted Person" allows users to connect their AI agents and tag-team tasks. • Some couples use it for shared to-dos or help planning surprise date nights. • While it cuts down on emotional labor, a therapist says not so fast: You still have to put work in. AI agents aren't just sneaking into your workplace anymore. Soon, they might be making regular appearances in your relationship. Since the launch of Instinct, an invite-only AI assistant that went viral among Silicon Valley insiders in August, early adopters have been using it to offload tasks like booking hotels and scheduling appointments.
text:
Instinct's new "Trusted Person" allows users to connect their AI agents and tag-team tasks.

Some couples use it for shared to-dos or help planning surprise date nights.

While it cuts down on emotional labor, a therapist says not so fast: You still have to put work in.

AI agents aren't just sneaking into your workplace anymore. Soon, they might be making regular appearances in your relationship.

Since the launch of Instinct, an invite-only AI assistant that went viral among Silicon Valley insiders in August, early adopters have been using it to offload tasks like booking hotels and scheduling appointments.

Then, on September 9, Noah Shinn, the company's 23-year-old founder, announced Instinct's new "Trusted Person" feature: You could now have your Instinct agent directly communicate with another person's Instinct agent to reduce the amount of "back-and-forth" in a relationship, such as coordinating plans and organizing vacations.

Introducing our Trusted Person network powered by our new Instinct-to-Instinct communication protocol. Your Instinct can now talk to other Instincts to coordinate plans on your behalf.Getting people together often involves a lot of back-and-forth: finding a time, working out... pic.twitter.com/LXkDpXGmea

- Noah Shinn (@noahrshinn)

September 9, 2026

So far, some users have found it helpful. "Instinct syncs with my wife's Instinct so we can actually finish a shared to-do list," Alex Borkin, a 36-year-old entrepreneur who uses AI across his portfolio of companies, said on X, noting that it was easier than manually setting up AI agents using Claude Code or Codex.

Have you used Instinct's "Trusted Person" feature with a spouse or partner? If you'd like to share your story, please reach out to jpugachevsky@businessinsider.com.

While Instinct may help eradicate the most annoying part of a partnership (figuring out dinner plans when you both keep saying "whatever you want!"), it can also open up the possibilities of new relationship drama. Some users have already reported some issues, ranging from privacy concerns to accidentally spoiled surprises.

Your emotional labor robot

The greatest appeal of Instinct and other AI agents is their ability to cut down on what Borkin calls "boring tasks" - like booking appointments or getting refunds.

"I close the loop," Borkin told Business Insider. "I get to go to bed and not think of 'Did I take care of jury duty?'"

Like other working parents, Borkin and his wife use Instinct's Trusted Person feature to smooth out their day-to-day life as a family with two kids, ages 3 and 20 months (and a third child on the way).

Most recently, the couple used Instinct agents to send them individual reminders to complete tasks for their daughter's third birthday party, such as ordering food.

"It's nice not having to remind myself of something I asked my wife to help with, and then remind her if she's taking care of it," Borkin said.

The more invisible work within a relationship - such as nudging a spouse to finish a task you asked them to do - requires cognitive and emotional labor. Some partners, more often women, can feel as though they bear the brunt of this work, leading to tension in the relationship.

Annie Wright, a licensed psychotherapist who works with Silicon Valley clientele, told Business Insider that this dynamic is so common in heterosexual relationships that, sometimes, even AI agents don't fully solve the problem.

"Even when you have an AI agent, who's putting in the prompt to begin with, who's architecting out the idea, who's remaining responsible for the oversight of that agent?" Wright said. More often than not, she said it's her female clients who are tasked with the burden.

Wright said it can also be tempting to use AI agents as a way to avoid enduring "weaponized incompetence" when a partner performs the task wrong - or just keeps ignoring you.

"An AI agent isn't going to bring that same relational scar tissue into the dynamic with you," she said. "It's very compelling. It provides a kind of shortcut, but it doesn't eliminate all the work for you."

Deep intimacy required

Instinct fans have used it to do everything from booking a birthday cabin to canceling forgotten subscriptions, impressed by its ability to successfully follow through on semi-complex tasks. Users can send Instinct a simple text request to book an in-network doctor's appointment, and it seems to follow through effectively.

There's a catch, though: Instinct needs to know a lot about you to perform well. Depending on what you ask it to do, it might need access to your email account, calendar, or even credit card.

Users have reported troubling incidents, including privacy and security concerns. Some users have also reported hallucinations and what appeared to be leaks of strangers' data.

Out of caution, Borkin said he only linked Instinct to his retailer accounts (like Amazon and Costco) without directly giving it his credit card. He also uses a throwaway email account for Instinct to avoid the risk of any sensitive information being breached.

Naturally, AI agent mishaps can cause new issues in a relationship. Wright said the biggest risk is one person in the relationship now feeling responsible for checking that the AI agent properly followed through on instructions.

"One partner thinks they've handed off a task while the other partner still feels responsible for making sure it happens - now you've got a new argument," she said. "Technology can become another place where you're disagreeing about who's responsible."

When agents remove agency

Sometimes, Instinct's glitches can be more innocuous - even entertaining. Luba Yudasina, an angel investor, said she asked her Instinct to help her plan a surprise for her boyfriend, according to her post on X. She wanted it to ask him when he was free and what kinds of dates he would like.

Instead, it blabbed too much.

Told my Instinct to reach out to my bf's Instict to plan a surprise. This is what his Instict texted him  pic.twitter.com/JqEM2IbzXm

- luba yudasina (@LubaYudasina)

September 15, 2026

On a bigger scale, using Instinct raises questions about the merits of smoothing out every crease in a relationship. If that idyllic proposal was entirely dreamed up and coordinated by an AI agent, is it as romantic? If Instinct handles all the household logistics and plans all the date nights because your husband can't be bothered to, do you feel as seen in your marriage?

Wright said AI agents could almost be stand-ins for 1950s secretaries tasked with buying birthday gifts for their bosses' wives. "Getting help expressing your care versus outsourcing the attention that makes the gesture meaningful - that's a really important distinction to draw," she said.

There's a high cost to cutting out any source of conflict in a relationship: the ability to grow together. One satirical X post by Alex Cohen, the cofounder and CEO of the AI agent platform Hello Patient, summed it up best: Who's to stop the AI agents from absorbing each partner's passive-aggressive jabs, the humans behind the screens becoming empty husks occupying a living room together?

My wife and I no longer talk to each other, instead our AI agents communicate on our behalf.This is the future  pic.twitter.com/b4mUhQpkK1

- Alex Cohen (@anothercohen)

September 21, 2026

It illustrates Wright's biggest concern: skirting over real relationship issues for the sake of expediency.

"If we're already arguing about how much time we spend with your family, having software arrange another visit hasn't really settled anything," she said. "It's just made a decision before we reached an agreement and really done the hard relational work to arrive there."

For some couples, there's work that even the top AI agents aren't cut out for. Michael Stothard, a partner at Firstminute Capital in the UK who uses Instinct with his wife, shared on LinkedIn that he wanted to branch out from using it for administrative tasks alone."Michael asks his Instinct to pass you a message: 'I love you,'" his agent said.His wife responded: "Tell him he's an idiot."

text:
A

fter 246 days in Hamas captivity, Israeli special forces rescued Noa Argamani and carried her by helicopter to a hospital outside Tel Aviv. There, a doctor turned to her and said, "Noa, we're really happy that you're here with us."

Argamani was confused. "The first thing I asked is, 'How do you know my name?'" she recalls. "I didn't realize the whole world knew who I was."

At 25, Argamani had become one of the faces of the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel. On the morning of her kidnapping, she was a college student about to begin her third year studying artificial intelligence. She imagined becoming a software engineer. Maybe she would start a company someday.

This month, she started a new job. Argamani has joined the venture capital firm Vine Ventures, which backs early-stage startups, especially in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and defense tech. She's working with Israeli founders and companies looking to grow their business in the United States. Her new role puts her contact list to work: Her ordeal thrust her onto a global stage, connecting her to world leaders and business titans alike.

"In this moment, if I want to learn and make an impact, VC is the right place for me," she says. "I want to be surrounded by people who dream big."

For Israeli founders, America is often the market that determines whether a promising startup becomes merely successful or truly enormous. Argamani sees herself as a potential bridge between the two countries - someone who can help Israeli founders turn their companies into global category leaders.

"My mission is to help Israeli startups go to market and really break this border," she says. If she succeeds, she could bring more of the world's best technology, networks, and business know-how back to her home country.

On an early fall morning, Argamani, now 28, met me in the lobby of Vine's New York office, clutching an iced matcha. She is willowy, her long dark hair falling down her back. In a blue button-down, faded jeans, and mules, she could be any West Village twenty-something on her way to work. She speaks softly and deliberately, holding unbroken eye contact. She flew into town for this interview before heading to San Francisco for meetings.

Argamani has spent much of the past two years being asked to revisit what happened to her. This time, she wanted to talk about what came after. Before we met, she texted: "This interview is so special cuz [we're] focused on back to life and rising from hell."

Hours after the initial assault on October 7, a mob of Gazans swept through the Nova music festival grounds looking for survivors. They found Argamani and forced her onto a motorbike. Someone filmed it. Argamani, eyes wide, her mouth open, stretches her arms toward her boyfriend and begs her captors, "Don't kill me." The video ricocheted across newscasts and social media, turning Argamani into an accidental celebrity.

This past weekend, Israel's military said it killed the terrorist who drove the motorcycle used to abduct her.

In the months after her rescue on June 8, 2024, she became a prominent advocate for the hostages who remained in Gaza, meeting with presidents and diplomats and speaking at events including the Time100 Gala. She stood in the gallery of the House chamber as Benjamin Netanyahu addressed Congress. She wore a borrowed suit; her own clothes stopped fitting after eight months of captivity.

She went back to school at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, a public research university in southern Israel. She found that artificial intelligence had remade the field of software engineering during her captivity. Models wrote better code. Digital workers, known as "agents," were starting to take on work once reserved for humans.

Argamani jumped back in. She and her classmates used large language models to scan news articles for patterns of antisemitic rhetoric, then map the countries where they originated. They built a website where users could pick a date and see where that rhetoric appeared most heavily. Through an entrepreneurship program, she designed a startup aimed at helping children with autism.

But the life waiting for her outside school had changed. "There's the person you were before October 7, and the person you are after," she says. Strangers stopped her in airports and crosswalks. She spoke on stages and shared glimpses of her life with her 201,000 Instagram followers: posing on the steps of the United States Capitol, gazing from the bow of a yacht, and video-calling her dad from her seat at the World Cup final.

Job offers followed. She could join a company or help start one. She could make a career of public speaking or modeling. A desk job no longer felt ambitious enough. She had access. She had attention. Sitting behind a screen suddenly seemed like a poor use of both.

"I felt that coming back to coding would be a waste," she says. "I want to do something with more impact - to make a change in the world."

Through her advocacy work, Argamani met Eric Reiner, founder of Vine Ventures. Reiner had spent his career straddling Israeli startups and American capital, first at Insight Partners, then at Dynamic Yield, an Israeli startup that used algorithms to personalize digital ads and websites, before its sale to McDonald's in 2019.

Reiner launched Vine to invest in companies on both sides of the Atlantic, but its edge would be in Israel, where its team would spot founders and help them reach into new markets. The firm, which manages about $500 million, has backed Israeli breakouts including Wonderful, Qodo, and Eon.

Israel has long punched above its weight as a startup hub. This year, Google completed its $32 billion acquisition of Wiz, founded by a group of ex-Israeli military officers. But the war had put the "startup nation" under strain. A 2025 report from the Israel Advanced Technology Industries Association found that 53% of tech companies in the country had seen more employees ask to relocate abroad, citing growing security concerns. After two straight years of decline, venture funding to Israeli startups is climbing again, driven by mega-rounds for companies including Cyera, HiBob, and Wonderful, according to PitchBook.

In April, Reiner invited Argamani to intern. Something clicked. In venture capital, she says, she could help more than one company at a time. She could use the network she had acquired to open doors for founders. And at Vine, whose footprint stretches from San Francisco to Boston to New York to Tel Aviv, she could help Israeli startups make the all-important jump to the US.

For the past five months, she has been learning the job. How to size a market. How to validate a young company. She helps founders pick apart another investor's "no." Israeli investors, she says, will cut a founder off mid-pitch to explain what is wrong. Americans tend to be more polite. "They can smile the whole pitch, but after that they will pass and never tell you why," she says. She started a full-time role in September and will split her time between San Francisco and Tel Aviv.

Opening her network is one way she thinks she can be helpful. Coaching is another. Her time in captivity showed her that a person can do everything asked of them and still have no control over what comes next. That's a fact of startup life, too, she says. "Sometimes, no matter how hard you work, things are not going to work out well," she says. She wants to help founders get through those stretches of uncertainty and understand what they can learn from them.

She insists she has always been an optimist, even, she says with a laugh, a "naïve optimist." That instinct, she says, helped her recognize the miracles that punctuated the darkest period of her life. She survived captivity. She made it home in time to see her mother, who died of brain cancer three weeks later. She watched surviving hostages return to their families. "After seeing so many miracles," she says, "it makes you more of an optimist."

But she has also seen how much can be taken away. She watched friends be murdered. Others remained in captivity after they were killed, their bodies returned months later in hostage exchanges. She went to funeral after funeral.

For Argamani, optimism is no longer simply a personality trait. It is a choice she makes in spite of the past - a refusal to let the worst thing that ever happened to her dictate what comes next.

"I lost a lot of people. I saw in my own eyes hell, being in tunnels, looking in Hamas' eyes," she says. "But I choose every day to have another part of my life, to look forward, to go to work, and not let the grief become my identity."

Melia Robinson is a senior correspondent at Business Insider, writing about how artificial intelligence is changing the legal industry.
